author: AfricanFeminism
title: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister and the Terms of Freedom
content:
Something changes when a woman occupies an office men have treated as their natural inheritance. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri’s

appointment

 on 29 September 2026 makes that change visible in Morocco. For women whose competence is routinely scrutinised, the pleasure is neither naïve nor trivial.


But the woman forming a government and the woman labouring in the fields, raising children without pay and denied an equal share of her inheritance encounter power differently. Representation changes who governs; emancipation changes what all women have the power to do. That distinction shifts our attention from PM Mansouri’s gender to the politics of the centre-right

 Party of Authenticity and Modernity (PAM

)

, which she leads. Will its programme redistribute the resources and rights on which women’s freedom depends?


The history beneath the headline


Calling women’s leadership foreign to Morocco requires forgetting its history. Historian Osire Glacier

documents

 women’s authority long before the contemporary premiership. Kenza al Awrabiya, the Amazigh mother of Idris II, helped secure the Idrisid dynasty, founded in the late eighth century in what is now Morocco. Zaynab al Nafzawiyya influenced eleventh-century Almoravid politics around Aghmat, near Marrakech. Sayyida al Hurra governed Tétouan, a city in northern Morocco, during the sixteenth century. Khnata bint Bakkar intervened in eighteenth-century dynastic politics.


Across the region,

Dihya

 is remembered as an Amazigh queen who led resistance to the Arab conquest in the Aurès, in present-day Algeria, during the late seventh century. Tuareg oral tradition remembers

Tin Hinan

 as a queen and founding ancestress of noble lineages in the Ahaggar, in present-day southern Algeria.


These histories expose how male authority is made to appear natural. Fatima Mernissi’s

The Forgotten Queens of Islam


challenges that selective memory. Colonialism also reorganised authority: French Protectorate administrators

reshaped

 customary courts around imperial priorities. What survives as tradition can carry the history of political intervention. 


Religious interpretation can give exclusion another claim to permanence. Islamist and other conservative opponents invoke this

hadith

 against women’s political authority:


«لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً»


Usually translated as saying that a people governed by a woman will not prosper, it becomes a prohibition irrespective of her competence. Asma Lamrabet, a

Moroccan Islamic feminist thinker

, questions turning a

narration linked

 to Persia’s dynastic succession into a universal ban. She reads it against the Qur’anic Queen of Sheba, whose judgement demonstrates capable leadership. Her argument contests male authority’s claim to divine necessity.


PAM’s promises and its record


Women have long contested how authority is distributed within the family. Fatima Sadiqi

documents

the Union de l’Action Féminine’s 1992 million-signature campaign to reform the Moudawana, Morocco’s family code. The 2004 reform abolished wives’ duty of obedience but retained unequal inheritance and exceptions to the marriage age of eighteen. Proposals announced in December 2024 left fundamental equality demands unresolved. In October 2025, more than sixty civil society organisations and public figures

joined to call for comprehensive reform

. Rights in Morocco have advanced through organised demands, not the gender of an officeholder.


PAM, a centre-right party founded in 2008,

advocates

 social modernisation and positions itself against the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD). It entered government in 2021 alongside the National Rally of Independents and conservative nationalist Istiqlal. Opposition to Islamist conservatism, however, does not itself entail reforming the laws and economic conditions that subordinate women.


PAM’s

2026 programme

 promises improved widow pensions, childcare, safe transport, a women’s enterprise fund and labour inspection. The commitments leave inheritance equality, abortion reform and decriminalisation of consensual same sex relations unaddressed. Mansouri called for

banning child marriage

 without exceptions in 2024, yet PAM’s electoral programme

omits that commitment

. Employment can support independence, but a wage does not cancel criminalisation or unequal property rights. The programme leaves those constraints intact.


Even PAM’s narrow promise to increase …

author: WoMin
title: Press Release | Women’s Climate Assembly strengthens Pan African solidarity, women-led resistance and the struggle for a just future
content:
“

Empowering women is a radical way to transform the world!

” –

Ivorian activist


The fourth regional

Women’s Climate Assembly

 (WCA), held in Yaoundé, Cameroon, from 5–8 October 2026, concluded with a powerful reaffirmation of African women’s determination to defend their lands, territories, livelihoods and communities, and to demand climate justice and reparations.


Under the theme, “

Our lands, our voices: African women united for climate justice and reparations!

”, the Assembly convened over 75 women community leaders, activists, feminist organisations, civil society groups and allies from twelve countries including Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Guinea-Conakry, Liberia, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Senegal and Zambia.


The gathering provided a vital space for women on the frontlines of the climate crisis, extractive industries, land dispossession and environmental destruction to share their experiences, strengthen relationships across borders and build collective strategies for change.


As the Assembly closed, one message rang clear: African women are not merely bearing the costs of the climate crisis. They are leading the struggle for solutions, defending their communities and shaping the future they want.


“

There’s an adage in my village that women cannot build a nation. The Women’s Climate Assembly has proved that women build nations. We counter this adage with the unity and solidarity of African women!”

 –

DRC activist-participant


Turning shared struggles into collective power


From communities confronting oil and gas expansion and destructive mining to women defending forests, seeds, water sources and ancestral lands, participants brought forward the lived realities of communities too often excluded from decisions about their territories and futures.


Through collective reflection, popular education and movement-building, women connected struggles that may take place in different countries but are rooted in common systems of exploitation, inequality and environmental destruction.


Designed by women activists and members of the WCA Steering Committee, the thematic teach-ins explored a range of political concepts, questions and practices, including:


The erosion of farmers’ seeds

: A challenge for building resilient and sustainable food systems. What solutions are there for preserving our seed heritage?  


Nature Commons

: The defence of the Congo Basin’s forests.


Counting the Costs of Mal/Bad Development and Demanding reparations

: The case of the African Development Bank campaign.


Fighting some of the false solutions to the climate crisis

: Gas extraction, enclosure of our forests and lands for carbon trading, green conservation and more.


Building democratic, accountable, ‘loving’ leadership

: Why are these principles so important to feminist leadership? What else do we feel is critical to leading as feminists?


Lessons on organising and movement building

: Growing National/sub-regional grassroots movements.


Building knowledge from what we know

: Building feminist popular knowledge as the basis for Building Women’s Power. How can we go about doing this locally in our communities and beyond that.


The WCA celebrated the knowledge, resistance and organising power of rural, Indigenous, peasant and working-class women. The

Each One, Teach One

 sessions embodied this spirit of knowledge-sharing, collective learning and liberation. On Day Two, participants exchanged practical skills, crafts and tools, sharing techniques for making baobab candies, producing eco-briquettes from cassava and creating seed bricks to cultivate and protect Indigenous seeds. Weaving, cloth-dyeing, beadwork and other practices also featured, affirming the value of knowledge held, practised and passed down through generations of women.


The gathering reaffirmed the importance of strengthening a Pan African ecofeminist movement that recognises the connections between the climate crisis, extractivism, gender injustice, food insecurity and the loss of community control over natural resources.


It also reinforced a fundamental principle: communities must have the power to determine their own futures, including the right to say NO to destructive development projects that threaten their lands, livelihoods and ways of life.


Climate justice means reparations, not empty promises

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: Mada Masr
title: Parliament gives Sisi mandate to back Saudi Arabia militarily, opposition rejects ‘blank-check authorization’
content:
Parliament authorized President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Monday to “take the necessary measures to support the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, following coordination between the two countries, to defend its territory, sovereignty and holy sites against any external attacks,”

according

to a statement issued by House of Representatives Speaker Hesham Badawy.


Lawmakers in the House, who had gathered for the third-closed door session on the matter in proceedings that began over an hour later than planned, stood in order to vote in support of the authorization, with a majority of two-thirds casting their votes in favor.


Twelve lawmakers from the Egyptian Social Democratic Party, along with four other opposition MPs — Diaa Dawoud, Atef Maghawry, Ahmed Farghaly and Abdel Alim Dawoud — refused to endorse the mandate, remaining seated during the vote, according to two parliamentary sources who spoke separately to Mada Masr on condition of anonymity. Lawmakers from pro-government parties voted in favor, they added.


Riyadh has made no official public statement, neither on Sisi’s request for parliamentary authorization nor on Parliament’s approval of it. Badawy’s statement, however, used the phrase “following coordination between the two countries,” instead of “if we are asked to do so,” the phrase Sisi

used

when he asked for the mandate earlier this month.


Saudi daily Okaz

used

 Badawy’s formulation in its commentary on the decision, which it said “comes within the framework of Egyptian-Saudi coordination on the security challenges facing the region.”


One of the parliamentary sources said that Badawy did not open any of the three sessions by reading out the proposed measure or the relevant constitutional provision, as is customary when Parliament considers a presidential decree, agreement or similar measure. Instead, he merely

asked

lawmakers to indicate their positions and vote on authorizing the president to take “defensive measures” to protect Saudi Arabia if Riyadh requested them, he added.


The same source stressed that parliamentary custom requires that lawmakers be given specific details — not shared with the press — including the nature of any mission assigned to Egyptian military forces that are to operate abroad, the size and composition of the force and the mission’s duration. None of these details was presented during the sessions, the source said. Instead, Parliament only gave the president authority to act in coordination with Saudi Arabia, he added.


The Constitution requires parliamentary approval when troops are sent on a combat mission outside the borders, making it necessary to provide lawmakers with basic information about the mission, the source said. Granting the president “blank-check authorization,” the source argued, is a contentious issue.


Egyptian Social Democratic Party member Freddy al-Bayady likewise told Mada Masr that no details were presented in either of the two previous sessions, as well as in Monday’s, on the nature and limits of the military mission, the duration and scope of the authorization, its financial and human risk or the risk of the conflict widening and affecting Red Sea and Suez Canal navigation. 


Bayady holds a seat in the House, butunable to attend Monday’s session as he was out of the country, he told Mada Masr.


He stressed that his party’s MPs stand in solidarity with Saudi Arabia and reject attacks on its territory, but need enough information to make a decision after weighing the consequences.


Egypt has previously provided military support to Saudi Arabia during Operation Decisive Storm in 2015, and to the United Arab Emirates earlier this year, without putting the matter before Parliament, the parliamentary source noted.


In their viewpoint, bringing the matter before Parliament this time indicates that the planned support could go beyond a limited deployment of equipment or troops, something that he argued compelled the state to seek out parliamentary approval this time.


Article 152 of the Constitution

requires

the president to consult the National Defense Council before declaring war or sending armed forces on combat missions outside the country. It also requires approval from two-thirds of the members of the House, voting in a closed session under Article 130 of the House’s bylaws.


In May, Egypt sent a “

detachment

” — a limited military formation drawn from one or several corps — to the UAE. Sources at the time said that the word …

author: Chan Tsz Yung Frederick
title: Laying on Thin Water: The Looming Danger of Sub-Saharan Africa’s Subsea Repair Vessel Deficit
content:
Submarine fibre-optic cables (subsea telecommunications cables) handle up to

99%

 of our global internet traffic and communications, underlining the operations of numerous businesses and institutions across the world. Their continued proliferation will bring higher network speeds and connect more people and regions to digital communications. Yet, whilst the world is on a roll in laying down more of this critical infrastructure, it is severely underequipped in properly maintaining them. Sub-Saharan Africa is no exception. As the region with the

fastest-growing population

 and a

large gap

 to fill in terms of internet connectivity, Sub-Saharan Africa is occupying an increasingly important position in the world’s network of submarine fibre-optic cables.


Sub-Saharan Africa in the growing demand for Subsea telecommunications cables repairs


Once a subsea telecommunications cable is laid, many potential costs are incurred: the future need for repairs due to factors such as human activity, natural disasters, and mechanical failure. Filling this role is the

registered

 fleet of 63 ships that has subsea telecommunications cable repair capabilities,

60% of which are not solely dedicated to repairs but are also cable-laying ships.

 For Sub-Saharan Africa, it is serviced by the

44-year-old

Léon Thévenin

, the sole permanent subsea telecommunications cable repair vessel stationed at Cape Town to care for the cables connected to this massive region.


Figure 1.

Photo of the

Léon Thévenin

 by Vessel Finder


It is true that many cables are soon to be retired, with

forecasts

 predicting the decommissioning of roughly 450,000 kilometers of cable over the course of 2026–2035. This means there will be legacy cables that no longer require constant maintenance or fault servicing. Yet, the laying of new cables far outpaces this retirement trend, with an expected 1,010,000 kilometers of new cable laid during that same time period. New cables carry higher technical resilience, but they remain just as vulnerable to external physical force, which

accounts for the vast majority

 of subsea telecommunications cable faults. Consequently, overall demand for repairs will likely increase rather than shrink. Following the global trend, a net increase of subsea telecommunications cables and subsequent faults is

expected

 for Sub-Saharan Africa. Major new subsea telecommunications cables are planned for Sub-Saharan Africa – such as

Via Africa

 and the

ReuNION Cable,

 with multiple landing sites in the region. It is imperative that regional repair capacity increases to match growing infrastructural needs.


Existing deficiencies in repair capacity


According to industry reports, Sub-Saharan Africa’s current situation seems to be fine on paper. In fact, it was

forecasted

 that only around one vessel is needed to cover not just the region but the whole continent’s repair demands. It makes sense if we are only looking at the amount of expected subsea telecommunications cable faults, but this is not the case as we take distance into consideration.


To illustrate how this relying on a single permanently stationed repair vessel is insufficient in answering potential demands in Sub-Saharan Africa,

a report by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) in July 2026

 highlighted how vulnerable this one-ship baseline really is through a hypothetical scenario where subsea telecommunications cable faults occur simultaneously near Mombasa and Dakar. One vessel clearly couldn’t cover both faults at the same time, not to mention the long transit time needed for the vessel to travel from one side of the continent to the other. North Africa is comparatively more well covered, such as by the

Mediterranean Cable Maintenance Agreement (MECMA)

, which provides two repair vessels based in nearby European ports to answer maintenance demands. And it should be noted that even so, the Mediterranean region itself is currently suffering from a repair vessel shortage.


Even though Sub-Saharan Africa is technically supplemented by several vessels that are based in other regions, the overall repair readiness has proven to be insufficient. Recalling the high profile case of the

2024 underwater landslide in the Trou Sans Fond Canyon off the coast of Cote d’Ivoire

, damaging four cables – MainOne, West Africa Cable System (WACS), Africa Coast to Europe (ACE), South Atlantic-3 (SAT-3). Under the ACMA (Atlantic Cable Maintenance Agreement) …

author: Sara Connors
title: First Nation of Na-Cho Nyäk Dun says it’s up to citizens to decide how to move forward on Eagle mine
content:
The First Nation at the centre of the Eagle gold mine disaster in north-central Yukon says it will ultimately be up to its citizens to decide how it plans to support the sale of the mine to a foreign mining company.

The First Nation of Na-Cho Nyäk Dun, on whose traditional territory the mine is located, indicated in an Oct. 23 news release that while negotiations with Singapore-based mining and acquisitions company Boroo are in the early stages, the relationship appears positive.

“Boroo has approached our Nation with openness, respect and good faith, and we recognize the positive foundation that has been established,” it says.

“We are not turning away from mining. We believe the answer is to do it better,” it adds.

The release says the First Nation is not granting any interviews for the time being.

A failure at the mine’s heap leach facility in June 2024 saw more than 300,000 cubic metres of cyanide-contaminated water released into the surrounding environment on the First Nation’s traditional territory. The mine subsequently went into receivership.

The Yukon government and PricewaterhouseCoopers, the mine’s receiver, announced last week that they had reached an agreement to sell the mine for up to $140 million, a process they said will include input from Na-Cho Nyäk Dun.

Officials said any potential buyer is required to have an agreement with the First Nation in order for the sale to proceed and mining operations to restart.

Yukon, Canada, ask for dismissal of $150M mining lawsuit launched by First Nation of Na-Cho Nyäk Dun

Singapore-based company chosen as potential buyer for Yukon mine after collapse

According to the release, the First Nation wants its citizens to have “the full picture” before it decides whether to support the sale. It notes that citizens “hold the highest authority” through its assembly process.

It says that includes understanding the environmental, technical, economic and long-term implications of the sale, as well as having the opportunity to ask questions before it makes an “informed decision.”

It also notes that the First Nation doesn’t want to be rushed during the process, either.

“Our administration, Lands Department, technical experts, negotiators and Council are working hard to understand the risks, strengthen protections and secure the strongest possible agreement for our people, our lands and the Yukon,” it states.

“If we get this right, Eagle Gold can become a story not only of what went wrong, but of how we learned, rebuilt trust and chose a better path for the generations who will inherit the consequences of our choices.”

The sale is not a done deal, at least not yet.

It still requires court approval and other conditions before Boroo can take possession of the site.

With the sale expected to close before year’s end, the release indicates it is a critical time for the First Nation.

“The most important work for our Nation is still ahead,” it states.

Sara Connors is originally from Nova Scotia and has a journalism degree from the University of King’s College in Halifax. After graduation she worked in South Korea for two years as an English language teacher and freelance journalist. After she returned home in 2019 she worked behind the scenes at CTV Atlantic in Halifax before joining APTN's Yukon bureau in July 2020.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Immigrant’s Death in Abusive Georgia ICE Facility Reignites Call for Its Closure
content:
Luis Sandoval was detained in a Folkston ICE center, where a hunger strike has been ongoing for over 2 weeks.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

An immigrant detained at an ICE facility in Folkston, Georgia, died on Friday, reigniting calls for the facility to be shut down and an investigation into the center as it faces an ongoing hunger strike protesting abusive conditions.

Luis Sandoval, a 48-year-old from El Salvador, was found with a “ligature around his neck,” according to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). According to the agency, facility staff found Sandoval at 1:46 am, and began lifesaving procedures. But he was pronounced dead at 2:28 am.

Sandoval, who was being held in the D. Ray James facility near Folkston, is the 60th known person to die in ICE detention since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term. He had only been in the facility for 21 days, having been arrested by ICE and sent to the facility earlier this month.

The Georgia Bureau of Investigation said that it has been requested to conduct an investigation into Sandoval’s death, per The Guardian, and ICE said that his death is “under investigation,” though it didn’t specify by whom. In a statement about his death, ICE highlighted Sandoval’s alleged criminal history.

Immigrant advocates reiterated calls to shut the facility down in response to Sandoval’s death.

Sandoval “should not have died in a cage owned by a company that gets paid to fill them. GEO Group and ICE have turned the incarceration of people into revenue streams,” said Murtaza Khwaja, the executive director for Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta. “This system that profits from human suffering will keep producing it. We demand a full independent investigation into Mr. Sandoval’s death, and demand that Folkston Processing Center be shut down permanently.”

The Folkston facility, owned by the notorious GEO Group, is already facing scrutiny over poor conditions. Earlier this month, roughly 500 people at the facility went on hunger strike, and organizers with the Shut Down Folkston Campaign say that 12 people are still maintaining the strike. It’s unclear if Sandoval was a participant.

Those on hunger strike say that they have faced torture, including solitary confinement and force feeding. They are protesting conditions at the facility as well as violations of asylum protocols, advocates have said.

On Monday, Georgia’s U.S. senators, Raphael Warnock (D) and Jon Ossoff (D), demanded an investigation and inspection of the Folkston center in response to the hunger strike.

“We are troubled by reports of medical neglect and retaliation by custodial officers in response to the mass hunger strike,” senators wrote in a letter to Department of Homeland Security officials.

“Reports from local advocates suggest that approximately 500 detainees are now participating in the hunger strike due to facility conditions and that at least thirteen participants have allegedly been placed in solitary confinement in response. If accurate, the use of restrictive housing to penalize individuals for reporting poor conditions would constitute retaliation and an abuse of disciplinary authority,” the lawmakers said.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Search continues for Gjoa Haven elder
content:
Ground searchers and a Canadian Coast Guard helicopter continue to look for a Gjoa Haven elder who has been missing for five days.


David Siksik went out on the land for a day trip on Oct. 21 and did not return home, Gjoa Haven MLA David Porter wrote in an email to Nunatsiaq News.


He was reported missing at 7 p.m. that evening, according to a hamlet Facebook post.


A Canadian Coast Guard helicopter

is searching an area about 45 kilometres northwest of Gjoa Haven, said David Lavallee, a civilian public affairs officer with the Royal Canadian Air Force, in an email Monday.


Nunavut Emergency Management initially led the search but asked the Joint Rescue Coordination Centre in Trenton, Ont., for aerial support on the weekend, Lavallee said.


On Saturday, a CC-130J Hercules tactical airlifter flew in from a Canadian Forces Base in Trenton and searched for Siksik until nightfall before returning, he said.


On Sunday, the helicopter

 continued to look for Siksik, as did f

ifteen ground searchers, in groups of twos and threes, according to a hamlet Facebook post.


The search has been complicated by difficult weather and deep snow, the hamlet said.


“Our brave volunteers have continued searching despite challenging weather conditions, including a blizzard that forced some to shelter on the land until it passed before continuing their search,” Gjoa Haven mayor Raymond Quqshuun said in an email Monday.


Community members have also volunteered to operate the local radio station and donated food, he added.


Nunatsiaq News did not hear back from Nunavut Emergency Management by publication time.

author: Valerie Anne
title: ‘The Hunting Wives’ Season 2 Trailer Has Sapphic Sex and Sad Exes
content:
Season one of The Hunting Wives was a wild ride, and I have a feeling season two is going to be even wilder. The full trailer dropped and it has me clapping and kicking my feet at the sapphic chaos about to descend upon us.

The trailer opens with Sophie’s husband asking if Sophie is “still dreaming about her” (“her” being Margo) and a few flashing scenes implies that yes, yes she is.

Other things we see flash by: a glam cowgirl photo shoot, Margo being manipulative to all kinds of people, and Callie being a sad ex and using a photo of Margo as target practice.

This show also knows exactly what it is and is leaning into it. For example, the song playing is Nancy Sinatra’s “Bang Bang”, which is the perfect backdrop for this trailer full of guns and sex and chaos. And the tagline for the season is “someone is going down,” which the narrator says while the visuals cut between a dead body and also a more…explicit interpretation of the phrase.

Based on how season one ended, I can’t wait to find out how Sophie ends up back in Margo’s bed (and her bubble bath!), and luckily we only have one month left to wait.

Check out the whole trailer here:

+ Bravo’s latest reality series looks like it’s channeling…The Hunting Wives in real life? Small Town Trouble: Texas, according to the trailer, features some women who are not-so-secretly hooking up with other women

author: Harlow Scott
title: Cancer in Prison: A Death Sentence?
content:
This essay is a 2026 winner of the

Keeley Schenwar Memorial Essay Prize

,

republished from


Truthout

.


How did my prison doctor miss a tumor the size of a doll’s head on my ultrasound? Why did I get cancer? I had been imprisoned at Perryville in Goodyear, Arizona, for 14 years — most of which were spent as a tutor, helping hundreds of women obtain their GED. So why me?


It turns out I was asking all the wrong questions back then, before my colon cancer spread.


When you are a cancer patient and a prisoner, you aren’t allowed any second opinions or alternative treatments, or even the right to refuse any of it. If you do, all treatment is terminated.


After the surgeon removed my tumor, my stomach looked like a horror movie connected by twelve inches of staples and yellowish pink flesh. He instructed me to keep my wound clean, but the correctional officers assigned to me refused to let me shower for seven days. Although there was a shower in my hospital bathroom, I had to take a birdbath while shackled. I was also denied any food for the first five days.


Any pushback against any order resulted in petty retaliation from the officers. For example, after questioning them about my basic human rights to a shower for wound care, I was denied access to the toilet. The female officer made me hold it for so long that I soiled myself and was forced to wear Depends for the rest of my hospital stay.


When the doctor released me, the only available transport vehicle was not outfitted for human passengers. Against my objection, I was made to ride in a windowless kennel for prison dogs. There were no seatbelts, which meant every hard turn or stop sent me slamming into the aluminum walls. For the first time I became claustrophobic.


Reflecting later on this traumatic ride, I also began to question the humanity of our Constitution. Specifically, the 13

th

 Amendment classifies prisoners in the same category as livestock property — so, why should we be surprised that correctional officers assume the right to treat and transport prisoners as animals?


So many of our bodies are undernourished, struggling to survive even when cancer is not attacking our systems.


By the time I finally returned to Perryville, I threw up in an oil drum. Because I had just undergone major surgery, I struggled to undress at the “strip shack,” where we must show our private parts to a female officer. This particular officer had a bad reputation for bullying prisoners and my sluggishness irritated her. She let me know it. As she searched my underwear, she stared disgustedly at it.


“Your chonies are stained,” she said, shaming me in front of another prisoner.


The stain was the direct result of another officer trying to humiliate me, and it was happening all over again. But I was too exhausted and in pain to care about the condition of my panties. I said, “I have stage three cancer and I don’t give a shit.”


Angered, she fixed me with a stare, roaming over every inch of my nakedness, leering repulsively at my body with such violation that it felt like assault — like someone had lopped off my private parts and freewheeled them into the trash can. While I was naked, vulnerable, and helpless, another woman weaponized her authority over me. I wanted to run, to disappear, but all I could do was look away from her glare.


On the upper corner of the wall was a sliver of light reflected from an unseen crack, and the wind outside made it appear as if the light was dancing. Pure, distilled beauty. It was free and I was not, so my eyes desperately clung to it.


Out of the corner of my eye, I could see the guard scrutinizing my scar like a grotesquery of spoiled meat, and I could feel the tears welling behind my eye sockets. I fixated wholeheartedly on the shimmering little light as though it was guiding me, showing me another way out. Suddenly I thought about the light spectrum, running to infinity in both directions. For all the darkness this guard wielded on me, it was not all-encompassing. There was also the divine spreading out three-dimensionally in light waves in the opposite direction.


I did not give her a single tear, and when she was denied an emotional reaction, she let me dress and leave.


Later on in the shower, I cried from a place deep beneath my heart where secrets hurt and indignities scream unheard into an empty black oblivion. I cried because I have a 22-year sentence and if I don’t give my pain an emotional outlet, I will die …

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Making Women’s History Part of the Curriculum
content:
Two teachers from Sacred Heart Preparatory School in California, Kristen Kelly and Serene Williams, have proposed an Advanced Placement U.S. Women’s History course in response to the issue of students not learning about women’s history. The courses would allow studying women’s experiences and contributions in greater depth. Establishing this course would create a better understanding of American history as it includes the diverse experiences of women and would help students connect the historical struggles for equality to gender issues today.

Women have contributed to shaping the nation’s politics, economy, and social movements, yet their participation is often overlooked by traditional history classes. From fighting for the right to vote, challenging discrimination, and advocating for female autonomy, women have had a significant role in building the foundation of the United States today.

One of the main arguments for WAPUSH is that women’s experiences are not explored in the classroom. In the article Educational Activism: Creating an AP U.S. Women’s History Course, Serene Williams, Kristen Kelly, and Clara Robinson explain that topics such as women’s suffrage and reproductive rights receive limited attention in the current AP U.S. History curriculum. The women’s suffrage movement involved decades of organizing, political campaigning, and resistance. However, teachers may not introduce this topic to students or have enough time to examine its strategies and leaders in detail. A dedicated course would allow students to study these movements more thoroughly and understand how women helped shape American democracy.

Women’s history is much broader than the fight for voting rights. The proposed WAPUSH curriculum includes women’s labor, politics, religion, culture, war, and violence against women. It also examines how race, class, sexuality, religion, and other identities shaped women’s experiences. This approach is important because women throughout the years have never shared one universal experience. Indigenous women, Black women, Immigrant women, etc., have faced different opportunities and forms of discrimination. Studying these differences would help students develop a greater understanding of American history and that America was not built on just our founding fathers, but by women who paved the path for opportunity and development through blood, sweat, and tears.

An AP course would also help students recognize the connection between historical events and current issues. The debate over reproductive rights and other feminist struggles today cannot be fully understood without examining the laws and political movements that shaped access to contraceptives, abortion, and female economic support. Studying topics from the suffrage movement to the Equal Rights Amendment can help students understand the political equality that has developed through activism and engage in feminist discussion. Learning this history would give students the context needed to evaluate debates instead of viewing them as different events.

Establishing this course would show that women’s history is worthy of advanced academic study. The WAPUSH campaign began in 2022, and according to its website, the campaign gathered more than 4,000 petition signatures and received encouragement from College Board leadership as it worked toward launching this course. Its proposal has also received university support, while the campaign continues seeking letters from high schools willing to offer the course. This continued support brings women closer to bringing light to women’s history and giving women a space in school systems and curricula. This petition is one step closer every day to its goal to educate and inform people all across America of women’s contributions.

An AP U.S. Women’s History course would make education more comprehensive, inform students even more about the history of the U.S., and connect past struggles to present issues. Women have influenced American politics, economics, culture, and social movements, yet their experiences are not always given sufficient attention in existing courses. By offering students an opportunity to examine these experiences, the College Board could help create a more inclusive and accurate understanding of the nation’s past. Women’s history is not separate from American history but instead an essential part of it.

author: Santana Dreaver
title: ‘Gratifying and humbling’: First Nation leads ghost net cleanup from Interior ‘B.C.’ rivers
content:
Volunteers Lyza Adoplh, John Redan, Nick Froese and Roxx Ledoux work to haul abandoned fishing gear out of the Fraser and Thompson rivers. Photo by Santana Dreaver


This article has been co-published

with the Narwhal

 as part of their

2026 Indigenous journalism fellowship

.


After starting the day with a prayer and a safety demonstration, a group of volunteers gears up in water-resistant clothing and lifejackets, ready to hit the water.


The crew is preparing to scour a stretch of the Fraser and Thompson rivers, removing any fishing gear or waste left behind. Fishing nets left underneath the water are commonly known as ghost nets, which trap and kill fish. 


As the saying goes on a volunteer call out poster, “ghost nets create ghost fish.”


TLKemchEEN (Lytton First Nation) has led the river clean-up program in the area for the past 20 years, all in an effort to preserve salmon populations and aquatic life following harvest season.


Over two days in September, a group of 40 volunteers spent a total of 20 combined hours on the water.


From Lillooet to Lytton during the first day, and from Lytton to Yale during the second day, volunteers passed through white-water rapids and rugged terrain such as the famously turbulent passage of Hell’s Gate.


When the raft leader yells “hold on,” that’s exactly what participants do, reaching down for a rope attached to the raft, laughing and hollering, ripping through the Fraser Canyon rapids. 


The cold river water splashes everyone — waking up the crew as countless bald and golden eagles watch from above.


“I didn’t realize how impactful everything is along the shores. I guess I didn’t realize that some leave their garbage and nets out there,” volunteer Rebecca Riley, who is from the Stʼatʼimc Nation, said.


“Once I saw that with my own eyes, I wanted to jump in and be a part of it.”


A newspaper ad about the river clean-up project inspired Rebecca Riley to get involved. She has helped remove ghost nets since 2018. Photo: Supplied by Rebecca Riley


‘That fishery is a communal right’


It’s a sentiment shared by many volunteers on the boat, who eagerly approach the shoreline when a ghost net comes into sight. 


Whether the net will take one person to remove, or up to five to pull out of the water, is unknown until people get their hands wet. 


During the non-rapid portion of the cleanup, countless stories were told, Indigenous people exchanged words in their languages to compare similarities and differences and folks even had hot chocolate along the shore, courtesy of Kumsheen Rafting, which was contracted to support the program this year. 


During the first year of the program, 126 ghost nets were collected.


“This year we picked up six nets and some garbage, some years prior we’ve picked up zero. We have to remind our fishermen not to be lazy and take their gear home,” Kevin Duncan told the Narwhal.


Duncan is an elected councillor for TLKemchEEN in “B.C.’s” Southern Interior, part of the Nlaka’pamux Nation Tribal Council. He has been involved with the program since its inception. He attended both cleanup days this year with his son, Aaron.


Kevin Duncan, an elected councillor for TLKemchEEN, has been involved in Lytton’s ghost net clean-up initiative since it started 20 years ago. He always leads a prayer before they begin. Photo: Supplied by Rebecca Riley


For TLKemchEEN, stewarding their waters as they always have is crucial — especially as salmon numbers decline. Life along the Fraser and Thompson rivers is deeply connected to salmon. And TLKemchEEn is home to where the two rivers meet, in the country’s largest salmon-bearing watershed.


“For future generations, sometime down the road, I’m afraid all they’re going to be looking at is pictures of salmon in a book,” said Duncan. 


The nets recovered by the program are given to those in need, including single mothers, low-income families and Elders from the nation. 


“As a Nlaka’pamux or Stʼatʼimc member … that fishery is a communal right, it’s not an individual right. It’s looked after by your nation,” Duncan said.


“Most times, you just get to see portions of the river from the highway, but once you’re down on the water, floating for eight hours from Lillooet to Lytton, it gives you a better perspective on where people fish.” 


Now 20 years into the program, volunteer spots fill up months in advance. Photo by Santana Dreaver


Removing fishing gear from the cold and fast-moving river can be …

author: Mehk Chakraborty
title: Inside the resistance to Spain’s crackdown on migrants in Ceuta
content:
This article

Inside the resistance to Spain’s crackdown on migrants in Ceuta

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


On July 30, images streamed across TVs, social media feeds and newspapers of thousands of people approaching a fence along the beach, in boats and by foot. Migrants, including children and families, were attempting to cross into Ceuta, a Spanish enclave bordered by Morocco. Facing violent border guards and the threat of drowning, over 70,000 people made it to Ceuta, with hopes of eventually reaching the Spanish mainland. Officials in Ceuta

said

 that 100 people died in the crossing — either by drowning or being crushed — and sources on the ground believe the number was higher. 


“I lost my phone, my money, my ID card, everything I had,” one Moroccan teenager recalled. “At one point I got pulled to the bottom, so far down that my feet touched the sand. When I looked around me, I saw women and babies who had drowned.”


“There was no proper humanitarian response from the local authorities — whether it is basic hygiene, food or shelter,” said Ric Fernández, coordinator and spokesperson for humanitarian and migrant advocacy group No Name Kitchen, or NNK, about the first days after the mass crossing. “Instead, there was an institutional response of pressuring people to ‘voluntarily’ return to Morocco. … There was repression, violence against people on the move in every form — legal, administrative and physical, and the forced expulsion of people.”   


Facing intense pressure and violence from both the Spanish police and military, within 96 hours most people returned to Morocco. Estimates about how many migrants remain are in flux, but the Spanish government

said

 in late September that up to 10,000 people are still in Ceuta.


While the global mainstream media quickly moved on from this story, the situation in Ceuta has

remained tense

 over the last three months, with increased violent harassment by the police, evictions and collective expulsions. In recent weeks,

“voluntary returns” and evictions

 from makeshift camps on the beach have ramped up.


Embed from Getty Images


Irene Estébanez Gutiérrez, a family and community doctor in Madrid, spent two weeks in Ceuta as a volunteer. “An information campaign has been waged that portrays people on the move as invaders, violent and dangerous,” she said. The

media coverage

, she believes, has failed to adequately address “the resulting humanitarian crisis, the systematic violation of rights, the lack of protection for minors, and the systematic violence and discrimination to which people are being subjected to, particularly by the military.”


Those who remain include Moroccan men and women, alongside Sudanese, Syrians, Palestinians, Malians and Nigerians. According to NNK, a significant number are minors. They are still stranded; the majority of them have slept in the street or in makeshift tents since they crossed into Ceuta over two months ago. 


Kora, who uses a pseudonym as an activist to protect her identity, arrived in Ceuta to volunteer in early August and found the violence and the lack of access to basic necessities particularly angering. The authorities were “not letting them access the supermarkets to get food or water,” she said. “They turned off the publicly and freely accessible water [to shower or drink] on the beaches and beat them or scare them in the middle of the night … to purposefully making their lives more miserable.” 


Organizing solidarity, facing criminalization


This

violence

, however, did not prevent activists and migrants from developing forms of organizing and resistance. Hundreds of migrants

staged a protest

 on a popular beach in Ceuta in August to demand asylum. On Sept. 21, Migreurop, a Euro-African network of organizations, activists and researchers that monitors European migration policies, noted in a

joint statement

 with over 100 organizations: “We have witnessed forms of resistance in everyday survival practices.” They mentioned the sharing of information, food and medicine, as well as safety and protection practices.

We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


Besides migrants’ self-led efforts, civil society has stepped up to help, with the Spanish Red Cross

distributing food

author: C4SS
title: C4SS Panelists on the Enduring Legacy of Don Lavoie
content:
The

Markets and Society conference

 this weekend (October 23-26) will feature many interesting panels on topics from public policy to self-governance to digital privacy to immigration and beyond. There will also be longtime C4SSers presenting.


On

Saturday from 9:00-10:30am

, Nathan Goodman is chairing the panel “The Enduring Legacy of Don Lavoie” featuring:


Cory Massimino – National Economic Planning: What is Right?


Don Lavoie argued in “National Economic Planning: What is Left?” that economic planning was inherently reactionary and thwarted genuinely left-wing aims like peace and liberation. Despite the prevailing conservative-libertarian fusionism of Lavoie’s day, his study of economics and history helped him see the transience of such an alliance: libertarianism was left-wing until the left became obsessed with economic planning and the right was always about militarism and hierarchy no matter how much libertarian rhetoric it adopted. Lavoie’s new (yet old) framing went under appreciated during his time and deserves careful reconsidering for anticipating the contemporary right’s increasing authoritarianism. This essay will build on Lavoie’s framing of economic planning as essentially right-wing, apply that framing to the contemporary American political situation, and argue such a framing is essential for any coherent conception of the political landscape going forward.


Jason Lee Byas – A Role For Lavoian Democracy


Don Lavoie argues for detaching our concept of democracy from the particular institution of voting, and instead seeing it as “openness,” or accessible means to shaping the world around you and its rules. An advantage of this approach is its complementarity with markets and property rights, which might otherwise be seen as in tension with democracy — thus partially reuniting liberalism’s “libertarian” and “democratic” commitments. Yet there is still a tension here. Philosophically, many libertarians may think that any social rules involving force should simply be set by natural rights, and so leaving these open to adjustment by anyone at all (let alone with open access to everyone) will be a problem. Practically, open access to reshaping the rules may spell uncertainty in problematic ways. I resolve these remaining tensions by suggesting a specific role for Lavoian Democracy. In short, many things are left radically indeterminate by any socially-practiced system of rights, and so too are many things left radically indeterminate by a commitment to natural rights. Questions of interpretation and resolution loom large, and the process of interpretation and resolution can either be hierarchical and authoritarian, or a product of ground-up contestation. There are principled liberal grounds — both moral and epistemic — for favoring the latter, and this is the role for Lavoian Democracy. I then offer a handful of institutions and practices that Lavoian Democracy might favor, including unions (of a certain form), adverse possession, and the common law.


Akiva Malamet – Beyond Recognition: Identity, Cultural Discovery, and the Limits of Social Planning


Scholars in liberal theory and political economy have long emphasized what Don Lavoie called the “knowledge problem”: social information is dispersed, local, emergent, and personal, and thus inaccessible to centralized or “high modernist” institutions. Lavoie and others showed that state economic planning fails because planners cannot access or generate this kind of knowledge and often undermine its creation. Liberal institutions, by contrast, enable people to align diverse plans and generate forms of knowledge no top-down authority could anticipate. I extend these insights to issues of identity, cultural development, and interpersonal life. Identity and cultural formation are bottom-up, organic processes reflecting the nuances of how people self-conceive, relate, and find meaning. State planning and institutional treatments of identity often obstruct pluralistic self-concepts and cultural discovery, flattening human diversity and complex individual lives into simple, legible categories. Ironically, formal recognition can perpetuate the injustices it was intended to remedy and reinforce intergroup conflict. State recognition of identity undermines the processes through which identity becomes meaningful, and conflicts with core liberal values of pluralism, self-authorship, and cooperation. Immigration restrictions present an analogous case: they …

author: Admin101
title: Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense
content:
Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN) is excited to announce the publication of

Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense

.


Drawing on organizing experiences of Black Rose/Rosa Negra members across the United States, this pamphlet explores how workers, neighbors, and communities are building collective resistance to ICE and defending their immigrant coworkers, classmates, and loved ones. By connecting struggles across workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods, the

transversal organizing

 approach we prioritize builds solidarity across different sectors of society to confront the interconnected structures of domination that shape our lives.


You can find a downloadable PDF version of the pamphlet at the end of this text.


Two Years of Trump II: Immigrants in the Crosshairs, Resistance Under Attack


Upon returning to office, Donald Trump wasted little time fulfilling his white supremacist campaign pledge of “Mass Deportations Now.” Via a flurry of executive orders and congressional acts his administration reinstated the reviled “family separation” policy; directed virtually unlimited resources to stop a fictitious “invasion” of the country’s borders; and sought to end birthright citizenship. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents blitzed Los Angeles in June 2025 with spectacular raids, followed shortly by similar operations in dozens of cities across the country including New York City; Chicago, IL; New Orleans, LA; and Durham, NC. This “shock and awe” strategy culminated in Operation Metro Surge, a months-long invasion of the Minnesota Twin Cities that deported over 2,000 residents. 


Meanwhile, support for the deportation machine plummeted as collective action against it swelled. Everyday people covered their cars, lawns, and lips with the slogan “Abolish ICE;” as of July 2026, nearly 50% of US adults support such a measure. Both May Days since Trump’s second inauguration centered immigrant defense in their celebrations. Rapid-response networks that keep watch for ICE, document kidnappings, and sometimes disrupt them spread wildly. Know-your-rights training flourished at worksites and community centers. Millions of Red Cards–wallet-sized cards outlining the holder’s constitutional protections around interactions with ICE and other police–were distributed at schools, churches, restaurants, and municipal buildings. Children and their parents caged in concentration camps went on hunger strike as constituents bombarded politicians’ hotlines and town halls demanding humanitarian treatment and release outside their walls.


Popular responses in St. Paul and Minneapolis demonstrate the possibilities of mass resistance. Like the Los Angeles Tenant Union’s community defense centers that countered ICE’s Southern California invasion, organizers reactivated dormant neighborhood networks from the 2020 uprising and began building new ones when word spread that Commander-at-Large Greg Bovino was bringing his paramilitary forces to town. Once Operation Metro Surge launched, everyday Minnesotans refined sophisticated systems to track, delay, and disrupt arrests. ICE agents retaliated by killing rapid-responder Renée Good and shooting Julio C. Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan immigrant targeted for deportation. Instead of cowering from the naked clampdown, neighborhood networks coordinated with unions, churches, and other civil societal organizations to shut down their cities on January 23rd. In its wake, Trump ousted Bovino and immigration enforcement plummeted.


But July 2026 saw record high immigrant detentions since Trump’s return to office with little public opposition. What explains it? ICE’s tactical shifts undoubtedly played a role. Bovino replacement and “Border Czar” Tom Homan traded provocative street operations with quiet detainers at jails and prisons and “targeted operations” at sites protected from activist impediment like airports. Escalating repression has also raised the costs of resistance. ICE’s bevy of brutality has included intimidation, beatings, and shootings, culminating in murdering Good and rapid-responder Alex Pretti. Federal grand juries fish from the shadows for information about our movements, stoking fears of informants that slow our organizing. From the Prairieland defendants to the Minnesota 15 and more, indictments and convictions on flimsy charges could make prosecuting dissidents even easier. Evidentiary discovery in the …

author: subMedia
title: White Nationalists Off Secwépemc Territory
content:
There is a growing white supremacist genocide denial movement in so-called Canada.

On September 27th members of the Second Sons, a white nationalist militia, marched on unceded Secwépemc territory carrying racist banners near a former residential school where mass graves of Indigenous children were discovered.

This action was timed to occur three days before National Truth and Reconciliation Day a flawed and limited attempt to acknowledge Canada’s genocide of Indigenous peoples.

The Second Sons are tightly connected to the so-called ‘Active Clubs’ movement and have called to remove non-white people from Canada at gunpoint.

The Secwépemc have a long history of resistance to Canadian colonialism, including the Gustaffson Lake standoff in 1995, and more recently, the Tiny House Warrior movement, launched in resistance to the TransMountain Pipeline project.

White supremacy is inherent to settler colonialism.

Settler anarchists have a special responsibility to support Indigenous sovereignty and confront white nationalists wherever they rear their ugly heads.

Get together. Crew up. Confront white supremacy in all its forms.

author: anred
title: El INTA exoneró a Virginia Aparicio: de investigar agrotóxicos a expulsada del Estado
content:
El Consejo Directivo del Instituto Nacional de Tecnología Agropecuaria (INTA) resolvió exonerar a la científica Virginia Aparicio, investigadora con más de 20 años de trayectoria que coordinó en Argentina el proyecto internacional SPRINT, dedicado a medir la presencia de plaguicidas en el ambiente, los animales y las personas. La decisión llega después de la suspensión de la difusión de los resultados, el retiro del país del estudio y un sumario administrativo que organizaciones científicas y socioambientales denunciaron como un caso de censura y persecución. Por ANRed


La resolución 366, fechada este lunes 26 de octubre, impone a Aparicio la sanción más grave prevista en el régimen disciplinario del empleo público nacional. La investigadora, ingeniera agrónoma y doctora en Ciencias Agrarias, queda fuera del INTA y del empleo público. La medida cierra, por ahora, un proceso que comenzó cuando los resultados de una investigación sobre agroquímicos debían ser comunicados a quienes habían participado del estudio.


Una investigación aprobada por el Estado


Virginia Aparicio trabaja desde 1997 en la Estación Experimental Agropecuaria del INTA en Balcarce. Durante más de dos décadas desarrolló investigaciones sobre plaguicidas, suelos, agua y prácticas para reducir el uso de sustancias químicas en la producción agrícola.


En 2020, el INTA aprobó su participación en el proyecto internacional SPRINT, financiado por la Unión Europea y coordinado por investigadores de la Universidad de Wageningen, en Países Bajos. La iniciativa reunió a equipos de diez países europeos y Argentina para estudiar la presencia de plaguicidas y sus mezclas en el ambiente, los animales y las personas.


Durante 2021 se tomaron muestras de sangre, orina y materia fecal de 73 voluntarios del sudeste bonaerense, entre productores agropecuarios, trabajadores rurales y consumidores. También se analizaron muestras ambientales, agua, suelo, aire y alimentos.


Los resultados registraron la presencia de distintas sustancias en las muestras humanas y ambientales. Entre los hallazgos difundidos se informó la detección de glifosato en la orina del 84% de las personas estudiadas. También se identificaron mezclas de plaguicidas, una cuestión central para comprender las exposiciones que ocurren en la vida cotidiana.


Estos datos no constituyen, por sí solos, una demostración de que cada sustancia detectada haya causado una enfermedad. El estudio buscaba caracterizar la exposición y aportar información para evaluar sus posibles impactos. Precisamente por eso, la comunicación de los resultados y la continuidad de las investigaciones resultaban fundamentales.


La reunión que no pudo realizarse


En junio de 2023, cuando Aparicio se preparaba para presentar los resultados a las personas que habían participado voluntariamente del estudio, las autoridades del INTA le ordenaron suspender la reunión. La investigadora tampoco pudo realizar la devolución de los análisis individuales en las condiciones previstas.


Seis meses después, el organismo resolvió retirar a Argentina del proyecto SPRINT y abrió un sumario administrativo contra la científica. La decisión de apartar al país de la investigación se produjo pese a que la participación había sido aprobada institucionalmente.


A partir de entonces, Aparicio debió responder por distintas decisiones vinculadas con la coordinación del proyecto. Entre las imputaciones figuraron el envío de muestras al exterior, el manejo de información confidencial, la intervención de personas sin autorización institucional y presuntas irregularidades administrativas y financieras.


La defensa rechazó las acusaciones y sostuvo que el envío de las muestras respondía al protocolo internacional, que los datos de los participantes debían resguardarse y que la financiación provenía de la Unión Europea. También cuestionó la proporcionalidad de la sanción solicitada.


El sumario y la amenaza de perder su carrera


El procedimiento se extendió durante casi tres años. La investigadora enfrentó ocho imputaciones administrativas y una sanción que no se limita a la pérdida de su puesto de trabajo: la exoneración la aparta del empleo público y compromete su continuidad como científica en instituciones estatales, incluido el sistema científico en el que desarrolla su carrera.


En septiembre, cuando trascendió que el organismo avanzaba hacia la sanción máxima, el caso tomó dimensión pública. Organizaciones de pueblos fumigados, sectores de la …

author: Redação
title: A democracia tem que ser defendida na unha
content:
O resultado do segundo turno neste domingo, uma virada inédita do presidente Luís Inácio Lula da Silva, demonstra que a política, como a conhecíamos, acabou de vez.


O

resultado

 foi fruto de uma mobilização cidadã como nunca se viu desde que as redes sociais se tornaram onipresentes na vida dos brasileiros. A campanha digital, mobilizada especialmente por meio de um canal no WhatsApp que concentrou 5% da população — 1 em cada 10 eleitores de Lula — demonstrou que, na era digital, a política se faz com mobilização e participação. Este engajamento conseguiu dominar a conversa digital, saiu das redes e foi para as conversas no bar, em filas de supermercado. Conseguiu superar o boicote descarado da Meta, Big Tech que tem maior controle sobre a esfera de debate público no Brasil — são 110 milhões de usuários no Facebook, 130 milhões no Instagram e 160 milhões no WhatsApp. Foi também a mobilização da sociedade civil que levou essa empresa a ser questionada pela ONU, intimada pelo TSE e investigada pelo Ministério Público Federal.


Os jornalistas investigativos — em especial os de veículos independentes — trabalharam obstinadamente, incansavelmente. Do caso Dark Horse às ligações de Flávio com o Careca do INSS, foi graças ao trabalho de nossos colegas que o público foi informado sobre o passado do candidato do PL, fatos de interesse público fundamentais para o cidadão decidir seu voto.


Aqui na

Agência Pública

, revelamos as

suspeitas

 de corrupção e omissão nos hospitais federais do Rio que eram o “feudo” de Flávio Bolsonaro durante o governo do seu pai; detalhamos

laços do amigo de Flávio

, Willer Tomaz, com o Careca do INSS; levantamos o

estilo de vida

 de Eduardo Bolsonaro e Paulo Figueiredo nos EUA, descobrimos uma

empresa que Eduardo abriu

 com o passaporte Italiano no Bahrein, apuramos as

medidas da Meta

 para prejudicar postagens da campanha de Lula. Mostramos como o assunto que mais afeta os brasileiros — a segurança pública — impacta nossas vidas. Revelamos

mensagens inéditas

 que evidenciam como Daniel Vorcaro, do Banco Master, mantém uma relação umbilical com figuras da direita brasileira, e também da imprensa. Foi nosso jornalismo que revelou ao Brasil a história da professora Vânia de Souza Borges, que perdeu seu filho, Rafael Borges, para o vício em Bets, no especial

Jogo Perigoso: o Brasil das Bets

. No meio da campanha eleitoral, Vânia foi pessoalmente pedir ao presidente Lula a proibição das Bets – e foi atendida.


Nosso trabalho resultou em ataques, intimidação e assédio digitais. Também enfrentamos o boicote da Meta — tanto pela redução do alcance do Instagram quanto pela censura descarada de pelo menos um post que denunciamos na véspera do segundo turno. Mesmo assim, as revelações que apuramos voaram: foram amplamente republicadas, embasaram episódios da série documental do Youtube Revelando, viraram postagens de influenciadores e memes.

André Janones transformou uma de nossas matérias em uma “missão” do Canal Exército do Lula, comandando a tropa a pesquisar a frase “FLÁVIO BOLSONARO ESQUEMA PANDEMIA”. O primeiro resultado a aparecer foi a investigação da

Agência Pública

. No último domingo, antes da votação, no debate da TV Bandeirantes, o caso virou um questionamento ao candidato do PL em rede nacional. ⁠


Neste momento, a recusa de Flávio Bolsonaro em aceitar a derrota e as denúncias de “golpe” por parte de nomes importantes da extrema direita vão fortalecer a narrativa de perseguição, de fraudes nas urnas e de uma suposta “ditadura”. Figuras como Nikolas Ferreira, Pablo Marçal e Eduardo Bolsonaro já começaram a dizer que a ampliação do período de votação constitui “roubo”. Os contra-ataques à eleição popular serão fortalecidos, ainda, pelo controle do Senado e da Câmara Federal, onde o partido PL obteve a maior bancada desde 1990. É uma bancada empenhada em desconstruir avanços como a proibição das bets, o fim da escala 6 x 1, a proteção do meio ambiente e dos direitos dos indígenas e a regulação das Big Techs.


O contexto pós-eleitoral se complica ainda mais porque o repuxo bolsonarista insere-se em um movimento global de forças antidemocráticas que querem matar justamente o tipo de mobilização cidadã que se viu no Brasil. Os EUA e seus aliados mais próximos no continente — como a Argentina de Milei — não reconheceram, até o momento, a eleição de Lula.


Neste contexto, nosso jornalismo será ainda mais necessário. Nosso compromisso é seguir investindo no jornalismo …

author: CMI Argentina
title: El batacazo de Lula, ¿la primera de una serie de derrotas para el eje Trump, Netanyahu y Milei?
content:
La elección en Brasil golpea fuerte a la alianza global de ultraderecha, que en los próximos días enfrentará dos paradas complejas: Israel este martes y el 3 de noviembre en EEUU. Sin brújula ni bajada de línea desde Washington, Milei sigue sin reconocer la victoria de Lula.


La victoria popular en la principal economía de América Latina puso un límite a lo que aparentaba ser un avance sin límite del bloque ultraderechista que a nivel global lidera Donald Trump, pero cuyas ramificaciones o poderes subsidiarios incluyen a Javier Milei.


En este sentido, la reelección de Lula también se puede interpretar como un reconocimiento de las políticas sociales frente al vaciamiento estatal, la reivindicación de los derechos ante la precarización de las condiciones de vida y la autodeterminación de los pueblos como contrapartida al alineamiento automático con los intereses corporativos globales.


Un mapa global bajo asedio y sin brújula 


El revés en la nación vecina expone la fragilidad de una entente internacional (¿Trump, Netanyahu y Milei, acaso?) que ahora aguarda con extrema tensión un calendario electoral complejo.


En cuestión de horas, el entramado ultraconservador enfrentará definiciones críticas en Medio Oriente, con la elección que definirá el futuro de Israel, mientras que el próximo 3 de noviembre la ciudadanía estadounidense concurrirá a las urnas en un escenario donde el liderazgo republicano acumula un marcado desgaste político.


La cadena de citas electorales pone a prueba la hegemonía de un esquema de poder que apostaba a consolidar su influencia a través de la polarización extrema y el disciplinamiento financiero de los Estados periféricos.


El repliegue de la Casa Rosada y el aislamiento regional 


Por lo pronto, el gobierno argentino no sale de su estado de parálisis ante el resultado en Brasil: habituado a tuitearse encima, Milei continúa en silencio y a la espera de un mensaje desde Washington, que aún no define si acepta o no la realidad o acompaña la impugnación del acto electoral que intentó ayer Flavio Bolsonaro.


Así, sin una bajada de línea clara proveniente de la capital estadounidense, el gobierno argentino profundiza su aislamiento político dentro del bloque sudamericano.


La semana pasada, durante la gira de Milei por España, ya habíamos visto otro signo de esta crisis en materia de política exterior, cuando ni siquiera los aliados ultraderechistas se dignaron a recibir al mandatario argentino.


La subordinación incondicional de la política exterior a los designios de Washington deja al Ejecutivo nacional expuesto ante el nuevo escenario geopolítico, evidenciando los costos de pretender subordinar los intereses soberanos a una agenda de choque ideológico en retirada.

author: Administrador
title: Preparativos Zapatistas para el Encuentro Abrazo con familias Buscadoras. Parte 3: CUIDAR, PROTEGER, GUARDAR
content:
Música: Meme del Real, «El mundo en que nací» Imágenes, edición y producción: Terci@s Compas Zapatistas

Compañeras Familias Buscadoras:

Les saluda el Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés, coordinador general de la Gira por la Vida – Capítulo México.

Pues les comento que seguimos preparándonos para el viaje que haremos para conocerlas, y escuchar y aprender de sus dolores y resistencia. Y para guardar su palabra en nuestros corazones y en nuestra memoria. Esperamos, de veras, aprender mucho de ustedes.

Acá donde estamos concentrados, de repente llueve mucho y hace frío. Está bien para quienes vienen en tierras frías, pero los de tierra caliente, pues sufren un poco porque no están hallados. A la lluvia todos estamos bien hallados, porque de por sí acá en las montañas del sureste mexicano llueve mucho. Montaña adentro, en las lomas y la selva, llueve hasta cuando no llueve.

Unas con frío, otras con calor, las comunidades zapatistas han mandado a prepararse a delegadas, delegados y 3 delegadoas. Hasta ahora 1530 según la cuenta. Tal vez baja la cantidad por enfermedades o asuntos familiares. Por ejemplo, una compañera se sintió mal, la atendieron y salió en el ultrasonido que trae cría en su panza. Tuvo que regresar, por razón de que estén bien ella y su pichito. Pero rápido, un compañero que le sabe a eso de los tacos (de hacerlos, no de comerlos; porque de comerlos todos, todas y todoas estamos muy bien entrenados), rápido dijo que él entra de relevo. Y sí lo aprobaron las comandantas y comandantes porque de por sí escucha las pláticas que se dan para prepararnos bien.

Aquí en el video les mostramos unas de nuestras preparaciones.

Sea toda la delegación completa, sea en las partes en que nos organizamos, nos preparamos para marchas si es que hay o para mítines que les dicen. En esas marchas, si es que se hacen, nuestra principal preocupación no es el rollo que digamos, sino cuidar, guardar y proteger a las familias buscadoras. O sea que no vamos a la bulla, a echar relajo, sino a escuchar su palabra. Y pues tenemos que ver de cuidarlas porque en su corazón tienen palabras fuertes, duras, que enseñan y orientan en la lucha por la vida.

Y sabemos que aprenderemos porque llevamos nuestra libreta y nuestro lapicero. Y hasta computadoras y tabletas y celulares. Y van compañeras que les decimos “Tercias Compas” que le saben a eso de la cámara, la grabación, la edición y la transmisión de los encuentros. Pero lo más importante es que llevamos la cabeza, el corazón y las tripas con ganas de aprender.

Ahí pueden ver, en el video, que se ponen unas compañeras con sus pichitos como si fueran familias buscadoras marchando por verdad y justicia, y luego nuestra delegación o parte de nuestra delegación, camina a su lado y luego las envuelve en un como escudo.

Y hasta el Comando Palomitas practica de hacer el escudo que cuida, protege y guarda.

De por sí así nos enseñaron nuestros anteriores, que nos dijeron que somos guardianes y guardianas de la tierra, la madre más primera.

Como ven en las imágenes, con tanto lodo que se hace en las prácticas pues ya casi no es que marchamos, sino que como que nos deslizamos. Como patinando pues. Y luego pasa pues que la chancla se quedó atorada, o el tenis, y no se puede parar porque atrás viene la bola, el bulto de compas. Y entonces pues ni modos, hay que esperar a que termina la práctica para ir a buscar en el lodo, dónde es que quedó la chancla o el tenis. Y pues mientras andamos como chuchito renco.

Compañeras familias buscadoras:

No vamos a pasear. Vamos a abrazarlas si quieren, y si no, pues también vamos para oír su palabra.

Lo sabemos que hay gente que está mal hablando de la gira. Dividen, quieren decir quién sí y quién no puede reunirse con nosotros, o sea que quieren dejar fuera a otros grupos porque no se llevan, y cosas así. Ahí después, otro día, el Capitán Marcos les va a decir de eso hasta con nombres.

Por ahora sólo queremos mandarles nuestros respetos y cariño.

Desde las montañas del Sureste Mexicano. Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés. México, octubre del 2026.
