author: Anikibawal
title: Lof Juan Currin de Temuco enfrenta una nueva orden de desalojo del único predio en reivindicación que queda de su territorio ancestral.
content:
Durante el mes de junio del año 2026, dos integrantes del Lof Juan Currin fueron denunciados ante el Juzgado de Garantía de Temuco por el empresario Pablo Jacobi Bauman por los delitos de Usurpación u ocupación violenta de inmueble, en el único predio que queda de su territorio ancestral, el cual figura en su Titulo de Merced. Los dos lamgen que se encuentran procesados en la causa son Leonardo Catrileo Chiguaihuan y Oscar Chiguaihuan Chiguaihuan, quien cumple el rol de Lonkopalife en su comunidad. Durante el mes de octubre, el lof y en particular, los lamgen Oscar y Leonardo han sido notificados con una orden de desalojo.


Este no es el primer proceso judicial que interpone el empresario en contra de la comunidad, durante el año 2001, Pablo Jacobi anuncio una querella por destrucción de propiedad privada, ante la negativa del Lof Juan Currin a la instalación de un cerco dentro del terreno que pretendía instalar el empresario para materializar un proyecto inmobiliario en el predio. Durante esos años, Mariquina Trecamán, dirigenta de la comunidad declaro que el empresario Jacobi tendría una visión parcial de la historia del conflicto, ya que este se remonta al año 1950, cuando Alfonso Taito Schneider llegó al lugar como arrendatario, donde instaló una fábrica de ladrillos, en palabras de Mariquina Trecamán «Este señor fue designado como tutor de un menor de la comunidad, quien al fallecer ambos padres quedó al desamparo. Valiéndose de esta situación, no sólo se apoderó del terreno del menor, sino que se apropió de casi todo el terreno de la comunidad Juan Currín utilizando distintas maniobras en tribunales» (fuente: https://mapuche.info/archivo/news02/austral010528.html).


El Lof Juan Currin lleva décadas resistiendo en este predio ante la usurpación y despojo de casi la totalidad de su territorio ancestral, arrinconados entre edificios y proyectos inmobiliarios han logrado mantener y preservar sus practiiicas sociales, políticas, culturales y espirituales, espacios ceremoniales como un un Rewe y Paliwe, ademas en el lugar se emplazan viviendas pertenecientes a las familias de la comunidad.


 A continuación, compartimos una declaración del lamgen Oscar Chiguaihuan Chiguaihuan, Lonkopalife de la comunidad:


«Bueno, yo soy Óscar Chiguaihuan. Hace tiempo atrás recibí una denuncia aquí en mi territorio, pertenezco a la comunidad Juan Currín. Hubo una denuncia hace tiempo atrás por usurpación violenta, según yo… le usurpé el territorio a Pablo Jacobi, me acusa de haber puesto un rewe, el rewe era de mi abuela y tiene más de 30 años,… me imagino yo que tiene, yo tengo 35 años… yo me crié ahí, siempre había un rewe ahí y el winka me echa la culpa a mí que yo puse un rewe. No es lógico lo que dice.

Esta comunidad es muy antigua, tengo documentos donde se registra la comunidad, el lof, el título de Merced tiene muchos años, documentos de 1922 hacia estos años, hay documentos de que la comunidad está asentada aquí en este territorio y sin embargo hoy día me acusan a mí de yo usurpar territorio donde yo he sido toda la vida de aquí.


Y pasa que después de la denuncia, hoy día llega otra mala noticia, de que el Winka y sus abogados pidieron una audiencia de urgencia en Fiscalía, no sé cómo se harán esos temas y llegaron un acuerdo de desalojar aquí a la comunidad, digamos, despojarnos de donde tenemos el Rewe, que es un lugar ancestral para nosotros lo tomamos como donde hacemos nuestras ceremonias, jugamos al palín, tenemos nuestra salida hacia digamos hacia la hacia la calle, mi familia circula por aquí todos los días y nos quieren encerrar prácticamente, nos aislarían, no tendríamos salida, nada. No entiendo lo que quieren hacer los Winka, pero nosotros queremos evitarlo realmente porque no sería lógico que nos dejen encerrados, sin salida, ni siquiera caminando.


Entonces pasa que salió la audiencia que pueden desalojarnos y nosotros estamos en contra y queremos apoyo, necesitamos que la gente haga visible todavía como el winka usurpa la tierra, se empeñan en despojarnos de nuestra forma de ser, se niegan a reconocer los que nosotros todavía hacemos, nuestro guillatü, nuestro palines, hacemos ceremonia, celebramos Wetripantü, entonces nos van a despojar de todo eso si logran su acometido los winka. Nosotros como comunidad, digamos, como familia siempre hemos sido afectados, siempre hemos tenido que estar luchando. Yo tengo 35 años, pero hay registro de lucha de mi comunidad mucho más de la edad que tengo yo, hay mucha …

author: Darío Aranda
title: Miguel Mirra: "Cuando la comunidad participa en contar su historia, la recupera para la lucha"
content:
Por Ivana Carino


Desde mediados de la década del 80 Miguel Mirra trabaja una filmografía que recupera lo que suele quedar por fuera del plano de las narrativas industriales: las luchas de los pueblos originarios, los conflictos territoriales y las resistencias socioambientales, entre otros temas. Director de cine, guionista y docente, se formó en historia y antropología antes de pasar por la escuela de cine de Avellaneda.


Nacido en Lanús en 1950, en el seno de una familia de clase trabajadora, Mirra relata su recorrido con calidez, humor y un particular gusto por las anécdotas. Entiende

la cámara como una herramienta de lucha

: no solo para registrar y visibilizar los conflictos, sino también para

construir memoria, poner en circulación experiencias y hacer cine junto a quienes protagonizan esas historias

. Desde

La máscara de la conquista

 (1985)

, hasta sus trabajos más recientes, hay una preocupación que atraviesa su recorrido: que el documental acompañe las resistencias y permita que quienes las protagonizan se reconozcan también en las imágenes.


Foto: Télam


Entre el documental y la ficción


“Llegué al documental porque no sabía hacer otra cosa”, bromea Mirra. En la escuela de cine de Avellaneda había dos vertientes, documental y ficción, y él probó las dos. Su primera realización con equipo completo fue una ficción de época ambientada en la mal llamada "Conquista de América",

La máscara de la conquista

, rodada en 16 milímetros en 1985, con escenas filmadas en Mar del Plata y Córdoba. “Para una escuela era un lujo”, recuerda.


Fue durante ese rodaje cuando comenzó a explorar el cruce entre ambos lenguajes. Había escenas que no sabía cómo resolver y decidió filmarlas como documental: “Les planteé a los actores que siguieran más o menos el guion y las filmamos en el aquí y ahora, donde había sucedido aquello”. El resultado funcionó mejor de lo que esperaba. “Me di cuenta que había quedado bueno”, recuerda. Allí comenzó a descubrir las posibilidades del documental.


Ese descubrimiento tomó forma con

Hombres de barro

, rodada entre 1986 y 1987, y estrenada en 1988. Mirra la define como “el puntapié” de sus trabajos como documentalista. Fue, dice, una experiencia extraordinaria. El equipo, de cinco personas, filmaba en las Sierras de Zenta, en el límite entre Jujuy y Salta, cuando se cruzó con una camioneta en la que uno de sus ocupantes llevaba una cámara. “Nos preguntamos ¿quiénes son estos?”, recuerda. Era Miguel Pereira, que estaba filmando

La deuda interna

 (1988).


A partir de entonces, Mirra fue y vino entre el documental y la ficción. En

Crónica de un extraño

 (1998)

 retomó la historia de Eulogio Frites, abogado kolla y referente del derecho indígena en América, a quien había entrevistado para

Hombres de barro

. Frites le había contado que su familia lo había entregado a la familia administradora de un ingenio, donde pudo estudiar y recibirse de abogado. A partir de esa historia, Mirra construyó un relato de ficción sobre un padre que viaja a Buenos Aires en busca de su hijo, un joven que se había alejado de su comunidad para probar suerte como boxeador. “Hay parte del documental anterior y otras son ficción”, explica.


Pero no todas las historias admiten ese cruce. En sus documentales biográficos sobre Adolfo Pérez Esquivel,

Otro mundo es posible

 (2010);

Darío Santillán,


la dignidad rebelde

 (2012); y

Norita, Nora Cortiñas

 (2013), la ficción no tuvo lugar. En el caso de Santillán, es categórico: “Ahí no correspondía meter ficción. Trabajamos con la gente que lo conoció”.


La exploración de esas formas híbridas continuó con

Fuego en Casabindo

 (2022). Mirra llegó a la historia a partir del descubrimiento de una ópera sobre la rebelión kolla de 1874 en la puna jujeña, cuando unos 2.000 kollas se enfrentaron primero al ejército provincial y luego al nacional, en la

Batalla de Quera

. La investigación lo llevó a escribir un guion que pone en diálogo la ópera con los acontecimientos históricos y construye un personaje ficcional que funciona como nexo entre ambos planos.


La película debía exhibirse en Casabindo, pero antes fue presentada en San Salvador de Jujuy. Mirra recuerda que, cuando estaba por entrar a la sala, vio llegar una columna de personas: eran kollas que iban a verla. Al finalizar la proyección le regalaron un pequeño toro de porcelana. “Es uno de los recuerdos más lindos que tengo de ese momento”, cuenta.

author: La Zarzamora
title: DESPEDIR A JUAN…
content:
Esta mañana nuestro compañero Juan Aliste Vega ha partido de su cuerpo, cuerpo que el poder mantuvo en encierro los últimos 16 años, cuerpo que practicó el conflicto y lo materializó en acciones armadas, que acompañó su vida en el álgido recorrido de ser él. Fue en el hospital penitenciario de Santiago, donde en compañia y calma, se fugó definitivamente.

Aún no podemos confirmar donde ni como será su despedida, ló que sí sabemos es que serán muchas, en muchos territorios, en las calles, en los puentes, en las jaulas, en avenidas y carreteras.

Juan Aliste es y será reivindicado, pese a los esfuerzos incansables de la prensa del enemigo y de sus múltiples intentos de desprestigiarlo, nosotrxs sus compañerxs sabemos que en este momento estamos despidiendo a un guerrero de gran envergadura. Pese a sus miserables conjunciones de palabras, el mundo sabe quien es Juan y en todos los territorios se levantará fuego en su memoria.

Que desesperanza deben sentir los poderosos, al saber que amamos pese a estar en guerra, que nuestra historia es escrita por nosotrxs, pese a sus asquerosos relatos oficiales, tan indignos como ellos mismos.

Hoy es un día de nuestra propia historia, hoy parte el guerrero combatiente que se alzó en armas contra la dictadura y la pestilente democracia de burgueses y traidores, el que no se dejó abatir, el que atacó y acertó, el que siguió compartiendo conocimientos y enseñanzas pese al encierro, el que enviaba notas y saludos, el que hacía llegar sus palabras a actividades y espacios.

Cada vez es más difícil despedir, esto no es una noticia, ni tampoco un comunicado, es nuestro adiós a un hermano…

A nosotrxs ahora nos quedará volver a mirarnos, tensionar el encierro de nuestrxs compañerxs, cuestionarnos y autocriticarnos, dejar de hacernos tolerantes al encarcelamiento, dejar de normalizar la sociedad carcelaria y hacer. Arduo camino nos dejas.

Juan que tu fuga sea eterna querido compañero.

Ternura y ataque frontal por ti y por todxs nuestrxs muertxs.

author: anred
title: Bolsonaro desconoce la derrota y Trump cuestiona las elecciones en Brasil
content:
Flávio Bolsonaro anunció que pedirá la anulación de los comicios tras perder frente a Lula da Silva por más de 4,4 millones de votos. Donald Trump también cuestionó el resultado sin presentar pruebas de fraude. La ofensiva vuelve a poner en escena una estrategia de desconocimiento electoral que ya tuvo como antecedente el asalto a las instituciones brasileñas en enero de 2023. La remontada de Lula descoloco la estrategia hegemonista del gobierno de Trump. Por ANRed.


El resultado de las elecciones presidenciales de Brasil abrió un nuevo conflicto político. El senador Flávio Bolsonaro, candidato del Partido Liberal (PL) e hijo del expresidente Jair Bolsonaro, se negó a reconocer la victoria de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva y anunció que recurrirá a la Justicia para solicitar la anulación de la segunda vuelta. La decisión se conoció el domingo 25 de octubre, luego de que Lula se impusiera por más de 6,65 millones de votos.


Brasil: Lula remontó 6,65 millones de votos, derrotó a Flávio Bolsonaro y puso a las big tech en el centro de la disputa


“Es imposible reconocer el resultado de las elecciones en el contexto en que ocurrieron estas cosas”, sostuvo Flávio Bolsonaro ante la prensa, al cuestionar una decisión judicial que extendió el horario de votación hasta las 19 horas en determinadas mesas electorales.


El argumento del candidato derrotado apunta contra el juez del Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) Cristiano Zanin, quien dispuso la extensión ante las dificultades denunciadas para trasladar votantes, especialmente en ciudades de Bahía y São Paulo. Sin embargo, la medida había sido solicitada por ambas candidaturas, incluida la del propio Partido Liberal. Además, la prórroga alcanzó a las mesas que continuaban abiertas, mientras que los votos de las que ya habían cerrado fueron contabilizados normalmente.


Los bolsonaristas bloquearon con autos el camino para impedir que pase el autobús con la gente que iba a votar. ¡Mirá cómo los sacan! Sea cual sea el resultado, lo que están haciendo los jóvenes brasileños para esta elección es heroico. https://t.co/MsQ8HS5Yqt


— PERIODISTA DE PERÓN (@PERIODlSTAPERON)

October 25, 2026


Flávio Bolsonaro calificó la decisión de inaceptable y denunció una supuesta ruptura de la igualdad electoral, aunque no presentó elementos que demostraran que la medida hubiera alterado el resultado general de los comicios.


Trump se suma a los cuestionamientos


El presidente estadounidense Donald Trump también cuestionó el resultado electoral brasileño. Según declaraciones difundidas por la prensa internacional, afirmó que en Brasil se había aplicado el “manual de Joe Biden” y sostuvo que los comunistas no abandonan el poder una vez que lo consiguen. Sus acusaciones tampoco estuvieron acompañadas de pruebas que acreditaran irregularidades capaces de modificar el resultado.


La intervención de Trump se produce en un escenario de estrechos vínculos políticos entre el trumpismo y el bolsonarismo. Durante los últimos años, ambos espacios compartieron discursos contra sus adversarios políticos y cuestionamientos a las instituciones electorales. La reacción del mandatario estadounidense refuerza el enfrentamiento político en Brasil, aunque no equivale a una presentación formal ante las autoridades electorales ni demuestra la existencia de fraude.


El antecedente del asalto a Brasilia


La negativa a reconocer una derrota electoral tiene un antecedente reciente en Brasil. Tras perder las elecciones de 2022 frente a Lula, Jair Bolsonaro mantuvo una postura de cuestionamiento al sistema electoral, mientras sectores de sus seguidores bloquearon rutas y acamparon frente a instalaciones militares.


El 8 de enero de 2023, grupos de manifestantes bolsonaristas invadieron las sedes de la Presidencia, el Congreso y el Supremo Tribunal Federal en Brasilia, en un intento de desestabilizar el orden institucional. Jair Bolsonaro fue posteriormente condenado a 27 años de prisión por su participación en una trama golpista, según informaciones difundidas por Reuters.

author: Rafael Oliveira
title: Com “exército” de Janones, Lula consegue virada inédita e é reeleito presidente
content:
Nunca antes na história deste país, um candidato à presidência havia chegado ao segundo turno em desvantagem e revertido a posição.

 Aconteceu. Com 51,78% dos votos, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) está

reeleito

 presidente do Brasil e vai exercer seu quarto mandato.


A virada improvável, que envolveu uma redução inédita na abstenção entre um turno e o outro (de 21,08% para 19,22%), tem relação direta com uma mobilização sem precedentes nas redes sociais – justamente o terreno em que a

extrema direita

 deitou e rolou nos últimos anos.


A tomada das redes pelo campo progressista – que transbordou para as ruas, com as maiores manifestações da esquerda em décadas em todo o país – envolveu vários jovens parlamentares que subiram ao palanque do petista, como Ana Elisa, deputada federal eleita pelo PT em Minas Gerais aos 21 anos e Érika Hilton, reeleita pelo PSOL em São Paulo. Mas nenhuma figura se destacou tanto quanto a do deputado federal reeleito André Janones (Rede-MG) e seu canal do WhatsApp “Exército do Lula”, que soma quase 11 milhões de participantes.


Para os especialistas em comunicação e política ouvidos pela

Agência Pública

, é consenso que a estratégia digital capitaneada por Janones foi central na histórica virada de Lula.


Jornalismo investigativo é antídoto contra a desinformação. Ajude a garantir informação acessível e gratuita para mais pessoas. Faça um Pix para

contato@apublica.org

 ou doe em

apoie.apublica.org

.


“O Janones entendeu a lógica das plataformas [digitais], no sentido de que não adianta só fazer conteúdo impulsionado e ou divulgado por influenciadores.

 O trabalho de formiguinha das pessoas para os seus grupos, das pessoas para as suas redes, é muito importante”, aponta Raquel Recuero, coordenadora do Laboratório de pesquisa MIDIARS (Mídia, Discurso e Análise de Redes Sociais) da Universidade Federal de Pelotas (UfPel).


A pesquisadora destaca que a estratégia conduzida por Janones também acertou ao gerar rejeição a Flávio – algo que a extrema direita vinha fazendo desde o início do terceiro mandato de Lula. “O que mobilizou foi a emoção, o medo de uma vitória de Flávio Bolsonaro [PL]. Não existe comparação com a campanha do primeiro turno. Foi uma campanha muito mais abrangente, digital, que chegou muito mais nas pessoas, já que, querendo ou não, o espaço do debate hoje é o digital”, diz.


Recuero destaca ainda a relevância da campanha digital em um cenário adverso para Lula no Congresso. “A mobilização é importante porque mostra que o presidente eleito tem força de mobilização, ou seja, tem apoio popular, isso pressiona o Congresso, pressiona as instituições. Mas vai ser um governo difícil”, afirma.


A pesquisadora Maria Paula Almada, codiretora executiva do Aláfia Lab e doutora em Comunicação e Cultura Contemporâneas pela Universidade Federal da Bahia (Ufba), destaca as circunstâncias em que a virada histórica ocorreu, com denúncias de interferência por parte da

Meta

 e, de acordo com a pesquisadora, com “o ministro

Kassio Nunes Marques

 agindo de maneira dúbia, muitas vezes juridicamente equivocada, favorecendo claramente um dos lados”.


“A gente viveu, pela primeira vez na história do Brasil, uma eleição das bolhas, em que a gente não tinha acesso ao que o outro lado estava consumindo e tomando como percepção da realidade”, diz Almada.

“A gente sempre soube da importância das redes e sempre soube que a direita domina essa lógica, mas o papel dos algoritmos, das plataformas e o não acesso ao conteúdo que está sendo disseminado do outro lado é um fenômeno novo”

.


Para a pesquisadora, o fato de Lula ter ficado em segundo lugar em um primeiro turno morno, com uma esquerda desengajada, fez com que as pessoas começassem a se mobilizar, encarando um papel de “protagonistas”, com as missões desenvolvidas por Janones no canal de WhatsApp, o que foi central para reduzir a abstenção.


Tatiana Dourado, pesquisadora e professora do Programa de Pós-Graduação em Comunicação da PUC-Rio (PPGCOM PUC-Rio), destaca a importância da identificação na campanha vitoriosa de Lula. “O que vimos foi uma mobilização em larga escala, com milhões de pessoas acompanhando canais de WhatsApp e produzindo e compartilhando conteúdos virais que geravam identificação, ampliavam o alcance dessa onda e contribuíam para consolidar convicções de voto, que vão se reproduzindo por contágio”, descreve.


Ela aponta que essa identificação, para além do conteúdo racional, tem uma expressão emocional …

author: Unknown
title: Şener: Flood disasters are not caused by heavy rainfall alone
content:
The floods that followed heavy rainfall in Istanbul last week have once again brought the destruction of the city's ecosystem and unplanned urbanisation into focus. The increasing spread of concrete development, the destruction of natural areas and the disruption of ecological balance are also heightening the risk of disasters.


At least four people lost their lives in the floods. The devastation in Ayazağa, where construction has expanded alongside the destruction of the Northern Forests, has renewed criticism of Istanbul's urban development policies.


Umut Şener from Polen Ecology spoke to ANF about the floods in Istanbul and the consequences of the destruction of the city's ecosystem.


‘The underlying problem is the city's lack of drinking water’


Umut Şener pointed out that ecological destruction in Istanbul has a long history and discussed the environmental problems the city has faced over the centuries.


Şener said, “In the case of Istanbul, it is possible to trace the transformation of nature as far back as antiquity. The environmental problems inherited by the Ottomans when they conquered Istanbul, following centuries of Roman and Byzantine rule, and the measures introduced to address them, demonstrate just how far back this history extends. The decrees concerning ecological matters issued during the Ottoman period, beginning with Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror, along with decisions made by the state bureaucracy and the legal authorities of the time, provide concrete examples of this.


The underlying problem is that Istanbul, surrounded by seas and with enclosed inland water basins, has faced a shortage of fresh water, particularly drinking water, since it first began to develop as a settlement. Over the centuries, population growth and expanding construction have added further problems to this shortage. Istanbul had previously served as the capital of the Byzantine Empire. When it became the capital of the Ottoman Empire, the existing problems were inherited, while the state's land-based system, implemented through conquest and settlement policies, contributed to the city's expansion and steadily growing population.


The destruction and pollution of wooded areas established to protect water resources, the discharge of rubbish and sewage into the Sea of Marmara, and the transformation of areas containing waterways and streams into residential neighbourhoods to meet housing needs were among the problems inherited by the Republic of Turkey from the Ottoman Empire. Of course, ecological problems that emerged with the development and acceleration of capitalism gradually turned into deliberate and increasingly intensive plunder of nature. Because the prevailing political outlook has never incorporated an ecological approach, these problems have become structural, compounded by new environmental problems, and continue to have devastating consequences.”


‘The effects of the Menderes era continue to this day’


Şener said that the plunder of Istanbul had been paved by the approach introduced during the Adnan Menderes era, which promoted the idea that “roads are civilisation”. 


He continued: “As is well known, Adnan Menderes is associated with roads. Roads were built recklessly to facilitate the spread of mechanisation, symbolised by cars in cities and tractors in rural areas. Of course, this must also be considered in the context of the Marshall Plan. Roads were presented as civilisation and development, but they also laid the foundations for the ecological problems that have become increasingly severe today. This was capitalist development that disregarded social needs.


A road was built along the Florya-Sirkeci-Sarayburnu route without any consideration for ecological, economic or aesthetic concerns in urban planning and architecture. Its construction involved expropriations that seriously damaged the cultural and historical fabric of the coastline, the building of seawalls and the creation of land reclamation areas.


The consequences continue today, from the disappearance of species in the Marmara ecosystem and problems such as marine mucilage to the destruction of public spaces inland, as seen in the Yedikule Gardens. These projects destroyed micro-ecosystems, disrupted water current patterns and caused pollution in water resources, including those flowing into the Sea of Marmara, to reach critical levels. The coastline was subjected to outright plunder, and that plunder continues.”

author: Kodao Productions
title: Activists ready massive protests against Trump
content:
Massive protests will greet US President Donald Trump when he visits Manila next month to attend the 2026 Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Meetings.


While the Ferdinand Marcos Jr. government is rolling out the red carpet for the US President, groups led by the Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) are organizing protests as large as those that greeted him in November 2017 to attend the same summit.


Malacañang appealed to progressive groups to defer their protests, saying “Filipinos should practice hospitality, welcome foreign leaders,” and to “air their grievances on another day.”


But Bayan rejected the Palace’s request, stating the summit cannot be turned into a “protest-free zone” for the sake of “misplaced hospitality.”


Bayan president Renato Reyes Jr.  announced that tens of thousands of protesters would be on Manila’s streets to denounce  the one they blame for triggering unprecedented surges in oil prices because of his war against Iran.


“Trump deserves our utmost indignation, the most intense of protests and the burning anger of Filipinos who have been severely affected by the US war in Iran. He is a racist, a corrupt fascist and the real scourge of the world,” Reyes said.


What is Trump’s biggest agenda in the Philippines?


Trump’s attendance to the summit, however, appears not to be his biggest objective. He and Marcos Jr. are set to seal the so-called Pax Silica agreement between US, the Philippines and about two dozen other countries during his visit.


Bayan said the agreement plans to put up a microchip manufacturing hubs in the Philippines for the production of US military hardware using locally-sourced rare earth minerals and local cheap labor.


Trump and Marcos would also reaffirm military plans that would drag the Philippines into the US’ growing tensions with rival China, Bayan said.


The group said the protest actions would also condemn US’ role as the main support of Israel’s genocide of the Palestinians.


“No red carpet for this madman, only red banners of protest. Trump’s image will burn in Manila the moment he steps foot on the Philippines,” Reyes said.


Sacrifices for Trump


This early, the Philippine Civil Aeronautics Board has asked local and international airlines to review their scheduled flights in anticipation of potential traffic and enhanced security protocols ahead to Trump’s arrival.


More than a hundred flights may be cancelled, delayed or diverted in the less than 24-hours that the US leader would be spending in Manila, a situation that will inconvenience thousands of passengers.


The Marcos government also announced road closures leading to the summit venue and when Trump visits Malacañang Palace for the signing of military and mining agreements before flying to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Schenzen. #

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

Activists ready massive protests against Trump

author: Ming-Yeh T. Rawnsley
title: Women and Taiwan’s Next Economic Transformation
content:
IN 2015, ECONOMIST Elliott Fan (樊家忠) encountered a result that his collaborators found difficult to believe. An experiment involving 450 residents of Taipei and New Taipei City showed no statistically significant difference between men’s and women’s willingness to compete. Studies elsewhere had frequently found men more inclined to enter competitive situations. In his Taiwanese sample, that familiar gap was absent.

Fan checked the procedures and sample but found no mistake that explained the result. The finding prompted a larger inquiry: what had shaped women’s opportunities and expectations in Taiwan?

Women’s participation in work, business and politics helped shape Taiwan’s transformation even as economic change opened new possibilities for them. That relationship matters again as the semiconductor economy enters the AI boom. Access to technology careers will influence who shares in its rewards and who helps direct its development.

In a podcast interview released in October by the NTNU International Taiwan Studies Center, in collaboration with the International Journal of Taiwan Studies, the National Taiwan University professor explored how agriculture, business, migration and electoral politics had changed women’s lives. His research suggests that gender expectations respond to economic opportunities and institutional rules. The same attention to those conditions is needed as technology reshapes careers.

TAIWAN, JAPAN, AND SOUTH KOREA share aspects of a Confucian heritage, including traditions assigning women responsibility for care. Yet their gender outcomes differ. Fan points to women’s visibility in Taiwanese politics and business as reasons to question explanations that treat culture as a fixed constraint. His experimental finding invites scrutiny of the circumstances in which gender differences emerge.

One explanation begins in colonial Taiwan. Sugar production expanded under Japanese rule, requiring substantially more labor than rice cultivation. Women became more deeply involved in agricultural production, increasing their contribution to household income.

Women’s contribution to household income could strengthen their bargaining position within the family. Yet they continued to cook, clean and care for children while taking on more fieldwork. Greater economic importance came with a heavier workload. That tension remains relevant to technology careers, where access to paid work may expand without a corresponding redistribution of unpaid care.

Nevertheless, demand for women’s labor could unsettle established restrictions. In research published in 2022 with Nora Cheng and economic historian Wu Tsong-min, Fan links expanding sugar-cane cultivation to the abandonment of foot-binding in early twentieth-century Taiwan. In the NTNU podcast, he also describes higher postwar female labor-force participation in former sugar-growing areas than in rice-growing areas, suggesting that changes in women’s productive roles could influence later generations.

These consequences do not make colonial exploitation a project of emancipation. They show how economic demands could alter household relations, with effects extending beyond the intentions of those directing development.

FAN’S SECOND EXPLANATION concerns Taiwan’s small and medium-sized enterprises. In a small firm, an owner may know employees’ capabilities directly. A capable woman may gain responsibility without passing through numerous layers of management dominated by men.

Family succession creates another route: daughters may take over when there is no son, when a son does not wish to continue the business, or when a daughter is better placed to lead. Across an economy with many family businesses, these decisions can create substantial opportunities for women to exercise authority.

Fan’s work on firm size and gender equity remains in progress, and small firms are not automatically fair. The important question is how business structures affect access to leadership. Applied to technology careers, this means examining how people are recruited, recognized and promoted, alongside encouraging women to gain technical qualifications.

His third inquiry concerns postwar migration. Military dependents’ villages, known as juancun (眷村), brought mainland Chinese migrants into contact with surrounding Taiwanese communities. Fan describes comparisons associating proximity to these settlements with greater female labor-force participation, later marriage and weaker son …

author: groundxero
title: ‘We changed the system’: how Serbian students ended Alexander Vučić’s 12 years in power
content:
“I see the glimpse of hope that this is our future and that actually we can say to our kids, our grandkids, we changed the system, we were the change.”


Gavin Brent Sullivan

 and

Tereza Capelos


 


Serbia’s student-led political movement has secured a historic election victory. Preliminary results suggest the so-called Student List has won 141 of the 250 seats in parliament, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party taking 104. The result brings the 12-year rule of Alexander Vučić to an end.


 


The Student List’s story is remarkable. It has no standalone leader and fielded candidates without political experience from across

Serbian

 society. Stemming from student-led protests against the entrenched corruption and

creeping authoritarianism

 of the ruling regime, it has now achieved an improbable dream.


 


In late 2025, one of us (Gavin Brent Sullivan) conducted focus groups with members of the student protest movement as part of the

Pledge EU Horizon project

. The project explores the emotional dynamics of political grievances and their democratic implications.


 


The protesters’ grievances were centred on the 2024 collapse of a roof at the newly renovated

Novi Sad train station

 in northern Serbia, which killed 16 people. Allegations of state involvement through corruption in the procurement process and lowered building standards have been denied by the government. But they nonetheless sparked large nationwide protests.


 


Focus group participants expressed anger and underlying fear about harassment during the protests by what they said were government-funded gangs. They also spoke of their concern at the threats and violence directed towards them, not only as they protested but also when walking in areas near government buildings in main cities. Several students reported feeling threatened even in their own homes.


 


At the same time, the students voiced dissatisfaction with teachers who were not supportive of their movement, and other students who opposed them. This dissatisfaction extended to older family members and relatives who repeated government-controlled media fabrications about the protests. These included claims that the students were being paid by foreign anti-Serbian groups.


 


Despite the fear of arrest or worse, and despondency that change could really occur, the students who took part in the focus groups were resilient. They were focused on their long-term goal of regime change, with many students talking with pride about creating a leaderless movement that was organising candidates to challenge Vučić in an election.


 


Several participants reported feeling spontaneous, intense experiences of national pride when taking part in the protests. Some spoke of taking back national symbols such as the Serbian flag to counter propaganda that they were not patriotic and wanted to destroy the country.


 


Feelings of solidarity

were also experienced

 when minority Bosniak Muslim students from Novi Pazar University in south-western Serbia joined the protests. As one participant said:


 


They’re a minority which was at odds with Serbia, with Serbian nationals actually. So now we had that part of reunification with them and they’re a Muslim minority. They are really active in these protests and student protests and it’s been wonderful.


 


Another member of the focus group noted that they expected elections to be “brutal”. But they were optimistic about the prospect of unseating the Vučić government. They said: “I see the glimpse of hope that this is our future and that actually we can say to our kids, our grandkids, we changed the system, we were the change.”


 


At the same time, most of the students did not dare to dream that they would succeed in ousting a government that had held a 12-year grip on power. It is stunning now after Vučić’s concession speech in which he admitted “it is clear that we have lost these elections” to know that they were successful just one year later.


 


What’s next?


 


The remarkable victory of the Student List should give hope to any group opposing a corrupt, authoritarian regime that a core commitment to democracy is precisely what attracts voters to choose progressive change.


 


However, while there will be euphoria, pride and tears of joy in Serbia as the election result sinks in, there may also be groups who are fearful of change and that the new government

may seek accountability

 for members of the ousted regime. Some …

title: Federico and Nelly Intise
content:
Spouses Federico and Nelly Intise are staff of the National Democratic Front of the Philippines (NDFP) from Maa, Davao City. They were together on October 26, 2006 in Calumpan, General Santos City when they were abducted and disappeared by suspected state forces.

author: Daniel Aloc
title: Ganggang ni JL Burgos bilang salamin ng lipunan
content:
Natatangi ang karanasan ng mga batang lumalaki sa kanayunan, malayo sa kalunsuran na may madaling access sa teknolohiya. Sa pagitan ng pagpasok sa paaralan at paglalaro sa mga burol at parang—kabilang na ang paghahanap ng mga gagambang panlaban sa kapwa gagamba—unti-unti nilang natututuhan ang mga realidad ng mundong kanyang ginagalawan. May nananalo, may natatalo; may nambubully, at may napipilitan lumaban upang hindi na lamang manatiling api.

Ngunit paano kung ang mga larong kinalakihan nila ay naging daan upang maaga silang mamulat sa karahasang umiiral sa lipunan? Paano kung ang mga batang dapat sana ay malayang naglalaro ay maagang nahaharap sa dahas, takot, at pang-aabuso.

Ilan lamang ito sa mga tanong na sinisikap sagutin ng Ganggang, ang kauna-unahang full-length narrative film ni JL Burgos, na unang ipinalabas sa Cinemalaya noong Agosto. Nitong Oktubre 21 ko lamang ito napanood sa Cinematheque Centre Manila, na ngayo’y matatagpuan sa bagong tahanan nito sa Philippine Film Heritage Building sa Intramuros, bilang bahagi ng Pelikula ng Bayan: Cinemalaya 22.

Hindi na katakataka ang tema at paksang tinatalakay ng pelikula, lalo na’t ang gumawa nito ay isang filmmaker na matagal nang nakatuon sa usapin ng karapatang pantao. Bago ang Ganggang, nakilala na si Burgos sa mga dokumentaryong Portraits of Mosquito Press at Alipato at Muog (2024). Ang huli ay nagwagi ng Best Picture, Best Documentary, at Best Editing sa ika-48 Gawad Urian noong 2025.

Hindi isang bagong proyektong biglaang nabuo ang Ganggang kasunod ng tagumpay ng Alipato at Muog. Ayon kay Burgos, isinulat niya ang kwento noon pang 2019. Sa halip na talikuran ang mga isyung matagal na niyang tinalakay sa kanyang mga dokumentaryo, pinili niyang ilahad ang mga ito sa pamamagitan ng naratibo ng isang pelikula—sa lente ng mga batang hindi pa lubusang nauunawaan ang bigat ng mga puwersang humuhubog sa kanilang buhay.

Sa pelikula, sina Ilay (Kenneth “Butchoy” Vincent Mendoza), Ten-ten (Don Rishmond Cerbito), at Mel (Raine Dela Cruz) ay tatlong batang naging magkaibigan sa paghahanap ng gagambang panlaban sa gagamba ni Anton (Prince Nathaniel España), ang bully sa kanilang paaralan. May kanya-kanyang pinagmulan ang tatlong bata. Anak ng isang desaparecido si Ilay, anak ng magsasaka si Ten-ten, at anak na naman ng isang sundalo si Mel.

Sa unang tingin, ang Ganggang ay isang pamilyar na bahagi ng pagkabata sa maraming pamayanan sa bansa. May tuwa sa paghahanap ng gagamba at sa pananabik na makita kung alin ang mananaig. Ngunit isa itong alegorya ng isang lipunang tila nakondisyon nang maniwala na kailangang maglaban-laban ang mamamayan upang mabuhay.

Sa talkback at Q&A session matapos ang screening, ipinaliwanag ni Burgos ang kahulugan ng tunggalian ng mga gagamba. Hindi naman likas sa mga ito ang mag-away sa paraang nakikita sa laro; inilalagay sila ng tao sa sitwasyong kailangan nilang magpatayan. Katulad ng mga mamamayang napipilitang mag-unahan at maglaban sa isang sistemang pinaghaharian ng iilan.

Sentrong usapin ng pelikula ang militarisasyon sa kanayunan. Binabago ng presensya ng mga sundalo ang pang-araw-araw na buhay ng mga residente, kabilang ang mga guro at magsasakang itinuturing na mga miyembro o tagasuporta ng New People’s Army (NPA) dahil lamang sa kanilang mga paninindigan.

Bukod sa karahasan at paglabag sa karapatang pantao na iniuugnay sa estado, ipinakikita rin nito ang epekto ng karahasan sa mga bata at kanilang pamilya.

Mahalagang banggitin na ang ilan sa mga karakter at eksena sa pelikula ay hango sa mga tunay na tao at pangyayari.

Isa rito si Rebelyn, ang gurong karakter sa pelikula na hango kay Rebelyn Pitao, anak ni Leoncio Pitao, na mas kilala bilang Commander Parago ng NPA sa Davao. Noong 2009, dinukot si Rebelyn at natagpuan ang kanyang bangkay kinabukasan. Ayon sa ulat ng Commission on Human Rights, ang biktima ay may mga saksak sa dibdib at iba pang palatandaan ng matinding tortyur. Ang sinapit ni Rebelyn ay isang paalala na ang mga taong hindi naman aktwal na nakikidigma ay maaari pa ring maging target ng estado.

Ang plaka naman ng sasakyang ipinakikita sa unang bahagi ng pelikula ay kapareho ng plaka ng sasakyang ginamit sa pagdukot sa kapatid ng direktor na si Jonas Burgos sa isang mall sa Quezon City noong 2007. Hanggang ngayon, hindi pa natatagpuan si Jonas.

Hango rin sa mga tunay na pangyayari ang eksenang nire-red-tag ng isang opisyal ng militar ang gurong si Rebelyn at ang kaniyang mga kasama bilang mga rebelde …

author: rti_admin
title: The Ahmedabad Reading Controversy and the Freedom to Read
content:
Who gets to decide what we should read? The question arose sharply in Ahmedabad this August, when two books were removed from a school reading list, and a silent reading session was later disrupted.

In August, an Ahmedabad school removed Malala Yousafzai’s I Am Malala and Anne Frank’s The Diary of a Young Girl from its reading list after objections from some parents and protests involving right-wing organisations. Later that month, a silent reading session organised in Vastrapur was reportedly disrupted by a group claiming affiliation with the Vishwa Hindu Parishad and Bajrang Dal. The gathering included students, lawyers, media professionals and others. The reading itself became the object of confrontation.

I Am Malala is the memoir of a girl who survived an assassination attempt after publicly advocating girls’ right to education. The Diary of a Young Girl records the experiences of a Jewish teenager hiding from Nazi persecution before Anne Frank died during the Holocaust. Whatever one thinks of Malala’s political views, or of the ways her story is interpreted, reading her memoir does not require accepting every view she holds. Anne Frank’s diary similarly allows readers to encounter the testimony of a young person caught inside one of history’s greatest crimes.

A book is not a political membership card.

Reading allows a person to encounter an argument without accepting it. A reader can examine its evidence, question its assumptions and reject its conclusions. The point is that judgement becomes possible through encounter.

Education is often described as the transmission of knowledge. But knowledge without the capacity to question it can become another form of conformity.

This question of who may read and what they may encounter carries a specific weight in the Indian context. For much of India’s history, access to formal education was deeply shaped by caste hierarchy. Ambedkar wrote that under the Chaturvarna system, the right to education was assigned to the Brahmins, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas, while Shudras were denied it. He also discussed the denial of education to women. The control of education was therefore connected to the wider system of graded inequality that Ambedkar analysed.

This was one of the structures challenged by Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule. Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule opened a school for girls in Pune in 1848, and Phule later set up schools for the Mahars and Mangs. In his 1882 testimony before the Education Commission, Phule criticised the concentration of education among the higher classes and called for a wider spread of primary and female education. His educational work treated access to knowledge as a social question rather than a privilege confined to a small section of society.

Dr B.R. Ambedkar’s conception of democracy makes this problem especially important. In Annihilation of Caste, he imagined an ideal society with “varied and free points of contact with other modes of association” and described democracy as “a mode of associated living.” For Ambedkar, fraternity was not sameness. It required people to participate in a common social world despite their differences. His writings on the Depressed Classes emerged from a context in which these communities faced restrictions on access to public wells and schools, and were subjected to social segregation and prescribed occupations. The “associated living” he imagined presupposes that those who were once excluded from classrooms are now full participants in the world of ideas.

A democratic society cannot expect citizens to form independent judgements while continually narrowing the range of ideas they are permitted to encounter. The democratic reader needs the freedom to examine an argument before deciding whether it deserves acceptance, rejection or further examination.

John Dewey understood education as inseparable from democratic life. For Dewey, democracy depended on communication, inquiry and shared experience. He saw education as a way of preparing people to participate intelligently in common life.

Not every book belongs in every classroom. Parents can question reading lists, teachers can challenge texts, and schools can make decisions about age, pedagogy and context. Citizens can protest. A democratic society must leave room for disagreement over education. The important distinction is between arguing that a book should not be taught and intimidating people who choose to read it. The first concerns the content and …

author: Sarah Raymundo
title: On liberal opportunism and the “purity” smear
content:
Photo from Naga City Tourism Facebook page

Accusing leftists and activists of demanding a “useless politics of purity” is a classic liberal defense mechanism designed to shift the burden of moral failure onto the critic.

Why did former Vice President and now Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo roll out the pink carpet for the Zionist war machine? When Robredo hosted Israeli Ambassador Dana Kursh for an official courtesy visit, she was not merely performing the routine gestures of local hospitality. She was actively welcoming and legitimizing representatives of the US-Israeli genocidal apparatus. This intervention centers an anti-imperialist analysis to dismantle the liberal apologetics surrounding this act. Rather than an isolated error in judgment, this diplomatic encounter exposes the persistent, foundational tension within the Philippine political landscape: the contradiction between liberal reformism and anti-imperialist national liberation.

Dismissing progressives’ critique of Robredo’s hosting of the Israeli envoy as mere “political purism” is politically and morally impoverished. The underlying mechanism demands a total, systematic critique. To understand why her defenders deploy the “politics of purity” accusation, and why that defense completely falls apart when examining real power dynamics and economic interests, we must lay bare both the liberal class position and the ideological sleight of hand at work.

To make sense of Robredo’s pivot toward imperial hospitality, we must look directly at the liberal class position. Her stance is neither an accidental misstep nor a personal failure of political intelligence but the direct expression of her class character and political alignment. Liberal reformism in the global periphery operates strictly within the legal, institutional, and geopolitical framework dictated by US imperialism.

While Robredo served as a focal point against the overt state terrorism of the Marcos-Duterte dynasties, her opposition was strictly intra-class—a feud over how to manage the neocolonial state, pitting rule-of-law decorum against autocratic violence.

Because her political legitimacy rests upon acceptance by the global capitalist order, her opposition stops at the border of imperial interest. When forced to choose between international solidarity with an anti-imperialist national liberation movement and alignment with the Washington-Tel Aviv axis, liberal reformists invariably side with the imperial core. They cannot critique the drain of value, the extraction of labor, or the military hegemony of US imperialism because their entire political project depends on remaining within that very apparatus.

This structural subservience explains why defenders deploy the “purity politics” weapon whenever that alignment is exposed. Accusing leftists and activists of demanding a “useless politics of purity” is a classic liberal defense mechanism designed to shift the burden of moral failure onto the critic. From a materialist standpoint, this argument relies on three ideological fallacies:

First, it replaces a materialist baseline with ideological absolution. Opposition to active genocide, ethnic cleansing, and imperialist aggression is not a performative or elevated ideological standard; it is the absolute baseline of human solidarity and anti-imperialist struggle. Labeling principled opposition to mass slaughter as “purity” redefines baseline morality as an unreasonable demand, attempting to pass off complicity as pragmatic maturity.

Second, it operates on the logic of liberal idealism, which treats political stances as abstract moral choices made in a vacuum. Political actions reflect concrete class interests. Shielding a public figure from accountability for legitimizing a settler-colonial state serves a specific political function: it conditions the middle forces to accept imperial violence as a routine, acceptable feature of global diplomacy.

Third, it trades scientific alignment for unprincipled unity. Transformative praxis distinguishes between principled unity—built on anti-imperialist struggle and mass interest—and unprincipled unity, which colludes with reaction to preserve electoral coalitions. Demanding that the progressive movement remain silent on international solidarity to protect a liberal politician’s image trades human rights and anti-imperialist consciousness for temporary electoral expediency.

author: chuang
title: “Every War Is a World War”: Interview with a Member of Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine
content:
The following is an interview with friends from Taiwan who have formed the umbrella coalition Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP). The interview includes an overview of the rifts in the Taiwanese left, and the frustration of TWAFP organizers carving out their place amid divisions between pro-unification and independence, or pro- and anti-American positions, in the contentious and highly polarized politics on the island.


The organizer recounts their efforts to confront Taiwan’s growing ties with Israel and direct support for the genocide in Palestine. They speak with sadness that, even as Taiwan is now the fourth-largest supplier of arms to Israel, surpassing mainland China, most Taiwanese care little for the distant genocide and the struggle in Palestine seems far away. And yet, TWAFP has led successful demonstrations, pulled together a broad coalition of disparate groups in support of Palestine, and conducted research to expose Taiwan’s complicity in the ongoing genocide.


Be sure to read their

report


from 2025, outlining specific pathways of material component support for Israel, including radar, armor, and an array of military hardware.


See also a recent

piece

 submitted to us, outlining Taiwan’s deepening ties with Israel under the DPP government.


–

Chuang


Q: To begin, let’s just set the stage. Over the last few years, the Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP) has helped to organize the largest mobilizations against the genocide in Palestine seen in Taiwan. Can you tell us a little about how TWAFP formed and maybe review some of the protests it has organized?


A:

Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP)

 was founded in April of 2024. Prior to this, Taiwan had already seen several groups doing Palestine advocacy work arise spontaneously, including Palestine Action Front, Taiwan Palestine Solidarity Network, and Parallel Government. As its name suggests, TWAFP is an “Alliance” that brings together groups that were already involved in initiatives related to Palestine. In addition to the three groups already mentioned, the alliance also includes a migrant worker organization, the

Taiwan International Workers’ Association (TIWA)

; the human rights organization, Taiwan Association for Human Rights; the cultural collective, Taiwan Rave & Punk Solidarity Front for Palestine; the gender issues group, Queer Margins; and the Christian group, Taiwan Olive Branch Peace Collective. From 2024 to today, we have organized one petitioning campaign, issued two open letters, held one candlelight vigil, hosted one book club meeting, staged five protest actions, held three press conferences, and organized three marches. In the future, we plan to engage in a number of other activities, many of which may be smaller in scale.


Q: TWAFP also did some very interesting research on material links between Taiwan and Israel. We can link to the report here, but can you briefly go over the main findings, and maybe go over any new information that you’ve found since that report was released? For example, have there been more details since then?

      


A: In September of 2025, we released our report,

Taiwanese Companies’ Complicity in Israel’s Ongoing Genocide

, which identified specific manufacturers assisting Israel in the production of military weapons, including via the production of components. For example: Gloria Material Technology Corp (GMTC) supplies superalloys and high-grade steel produced through electroslag remelting, while ADLINK Technology supplies embedded computing systems and industrial-grade computers. In another case, Transcom marketed its vertically integrated capabilities—spanning chip design to module production—to enter the Israeli defense supply chain and is now a key, long-term supplier of components for the EL/M-2084 multi-mission radar, which is a core element of the Israeli “Iron Dome” air defense system designed by Israeli defense company Elta.


Since the primary purpose of this report was to provide accurate information that could be used by media outlets and other organizations, who would ideally follow up with their own reporting and investigation, we were relatively restrained in our writing approach and did not engage in much interpretation or extrapolation. author: Unknown
title: PJAK spokesperson Awdanan: Region preparing for new phase of war
content:
Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK) spokesperson Rêwar Awdanan commented on the course of the war between Iran, the US and Israel, as well as developments across the region.


PJAK spokesperson Rêwar Awdanan noted that the Islamic Republic of Iran had suffered devastating defeats in the 12-Day War, the 40-Day War and the Strait of Hormuz War. “Despite this, it continues to act stubbornly and ignores the advice of figures such as Karroubi, Khatami, Zarif and Rouhani. They even view agreements such as the Treaty of Turkmenchay as beneficial to the stability of the system. Negotiations and the Islamabad Agreement were not enough to extinguish the flames of war, because the concessions demanded by each side are unacceptable to the other,” he said.


Negotiations failed to prevent war


Stating that all indications point to preparations for a new phase in the US-Israeli war against the Islamic Republic of Iran, Awdanan said: “The Strait of Hormuz War and the naval and air blockade imposed on Iran demonstrate the reality of the full-scale and intense war we are facing. In the phase preceding the conflict, neither the Islamic Republic of Iran was able to impose on the US and Israel the share of power it wanted in the new Middle Eastern political system, security arrangements, and the region’s trade and economic routes, nor did the US and Israel succeed in bringing the regime under control and completely destroying it through military attacks and the targeting of Ali Khamenei and other leaders. Removing the Islamic Republic of Iran from its position as a dangerous power within the new Middle Eastern order is a fundamental part of the US strategy to contain China.”


This time, things will be different


Noting that the global economy would weaken, and the US would be unable to advance its agenda against China as long as the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb remained under the control of the Islamic Republic and its proxy forces, Awdanan said: “By easing pressure on Russia and reducing its support for Ukraine, Trump is effectively pressuring the European powers—Britain, France and Germany—not to stand in the way of the US-Israeli agenda in the war against the Islamic Republic. Neither the Islamic Republic nor the US had committed all its forces during the previous stages of the war. This time, however, things will be different.”


We may witness a new form of World War III


Awdanan stated that the war would intensify, and strategic infrastructure would suffer further destruction. “Current indications suggest that we may witness a new form of World War III. The scope of the war will encompass the areas surrounding Iran, particularly the countries of the Arabian Peninsula. The region is currently in turmoil, and the parties are ready at any moment to unleash a living hell upon one another,” he said.

author: Kodao Productions
title: Libel, cyberlibel’s real intent
content:
By

Atty. Ephraim B. Cortez


Libel and cyber libel are being weaponized to intimidate journalists and undermine press freedom.


Late last week, Pulong Duterte filed a criminal complaint for cyber libel naming several journalists among the respondents. He filed the criminal complaint in Davao City. A few days later, a Davao City court issued a warrant of arrest for cyber libel, and veteran journalist Philip Lustre was arrested.  These charges appear to be fabricated and intended to intimidate journalists.


Mr. Lustre’s case exemplifies a fabricated charge and should raise concerns about the actions of both the prosecutor’s office and the court.


Some argue that the Court is not at fault for issuing the warrant of arrest, as it is a procedural step, and is automatically issued, after the case is raffled. However, both the prosecutor’s office and the Court share responsibility.


It appears that Mr. Lustre was not given the opportunity to participate in the Preliminary Investigation. The investigating prosecutor proceeded without proof that Mr. Lustre was properly notified via subpoena. This raises concerns about whether respondents are properly served at their address. In Mr. Lustre’s case, as a prominent journalist based in Metro Manila, authorities knew where to serve the warrant, making the lack of subpoena service particularly concerning.


This practice, of proceeding with the investigation whether the respondent received the subpoena or not, is highly irregular and violates the due process rights of the respondent.


As regards the issuing Judge, the 1987 Constitution’s provision is clear and unambiguous. Art. III, Sec. 2 requires that “no search warrant or warrant of arrest shall issue except upon PROBABLE CAUSE to be DETERMINED PERSONALLY BY THE JUDGE AFTER EXAMINATION UNDER OATH OR AFFIRMATION OF THE COMPLAINANT AND THE WITNESSES HE MAY PRODUCE, and particularly describing the place to be searched and the persons or things to be seized” (emphasis supplied). Section 6(a), Rule 112 requires that within ten days after a criminal case is raffled to a court, the Presiding Judge evaluate the prosecution’s resolution and the supporting evidence. Based on the Judge’s personal evaluation, he may “immediately dismiss the case if the evidence on record clearly fails to establish probable cause. If he finds probable cause, he shall issue a warrant of arrest.” In the exercise of his discretion whether to issue a warrant of arrest or not, the Judge is required that:


“x x x before issuing a warrant of arrest, must satisfy himself that based on the evidence submitted there is sufficient proof that a crime has been committed and that the person to be arrested is probably guilty thereof.’” (Doris Tereso Ho vs. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 106632, Oct. 9, 1997)


Warrants of arrest are not automatically issued upon filing of the criminal Information. It may only be issued if there is probable cause to justify such issuance. If there is no probable cause, the judge may end the litigation there. The Supreme Court’s admonition in Salonga vs. Cruz Pano guides our Courts in resolving issues of probable cause. The Supreme Court ruled in Salonga vs. Cruz Pano (G.R. No. L-59524, Feb. 18, 1985) that:


“It is imperative upon the fiscal or the judge, as the case may be, to relieve the accused from the pain of going through a trial once it is ascertained that the evidence is insufficient to sustain a prima facie case or that no probable cause exists to form a sufficient belief as to the guilt of the accused.”


Fabricated charges persist when duty bearers, including police, prosecutors, and judges, allow them to proceed. Such cases advance through the justice system only when the investigating prosecutors find probable cause and the Court allows them to proceed, despite their questionable basis.


Libel and cyberlibel are increasingly used to intimidate journalists and restrict free expression and press freedom. The use of libel and cyber libel against journalists becomes more lethal and chilling when justice system officials fail to follow proper procedures, whether intentionally or not, allowing trumped up cases to prosper.


This is not about the possibility of the “accused” being acquitted after trial on the merits. The issue boils down to exposing an innocent man to the rigors of a full-blown trial when it can be nipped in the bud at the very start. According to the Supreme Court, the right to be free includes protection …

author: Brian Hioe
title: Labor Groups Seek to Put Demands on Agenda Ahead of Election
content:
TAIWAN HAS SEEN a number of labor demonstrations in recent weeks.

A strike by workers at iconic snack Kuai Kuai’s Zhongli factory came to an end after five days earlier this month. Kuai Kuai is an iconic snack best known for a superstition that keeping bags of it near machinery keeps them running smoothly. Kuai Kuai operates one factory in Taoyuan, but 130 out of 155 union members voted in favor of a strike after the company decided to relocate to Hsinchu.

The two sites are 39 kilometers from each other, meaning that the move is untenable for many workers. Workers were only informed of the land scale on September 1st. According to the Ministry of Labor, the move was not expected for another two years. The factory has operated in Zhongli since 1968, and 1/3rd of workers at Kuai Kuai have worked there for more than thirty years, despite the fact that their wages are near minimum wage.

Though workers initially voted only for a one-day strike, the action was later extended indefinitely. After the strike, workers won four months’ wages plus severance pay if they are reassigned in the Zhongli factory and eight months’ wages plus severance pay if they have to leave their jobs because of the planned reassignment to Hsinchu and resign by September 30, 2028. Workers with twelve years of experience under the labor pension system will receive a further 100,000 NT. Kuai Kuai has stated that it will not lay off workers for two years and that workers who are laid off afterward will receive two months’ wages.

Workers have accused the San-Ti Group that owns Kuai Kuai of perhaps having only acquired the company with an eye on selling its land to Advanced Semiconductor Engineering Inc. Originally, Kuai Kuai workers were only offered a 5% pay increase and verbal assurances that they would be relocated to the new factory. It is to be seen if acquiring land to sell it to technology companies is a tactic increasingly adopted in corporate acquisitions going forward.

To this extent, migrant worker groups have criticized Singaporean company Sheffield Green and Indonesian company PT Kepodang Makmur Sejahtera, both offshore wind manufacturers, of violating the contracts of Indonesian migrant workers. Specifically, despite being skilled workers as fitters, such workers signed contracts that promised pay of 48,000 NT per month, but were later only paid between 100 NT and 143 NT per month. Such groups demonstrated earlier this month.

Such workers were part of projects run by Taiwanese company Century Energy Co., Ltd., but Century Energy has skirted responsibility by stating that it had no responsibility over contracts signed between workers and foreign contractors under a “contract performance” system that allows the company to bring over foreign workers to be part of projects. Under this system, the Indonesian workers were paid less than the minimum salary in the Labor Standards Act.

In response to such criticism, the Ministry of Labor has stated that it will step up inspections. It is to be seen if this actually takes place.

Likewise, the May 1 Action Alliance–a coalition of labor groups–demonstrated outside of the Executive Yuan on October 13th to call for employers to increase the amount of money they contribute to worker pensions. The Action Alliance cited that the mandatory employer contribution rate had remained at 6% since the current pension system was introduced in 2005, though expectations were originally that the rate would increase. As such, calls by labor groups were for the contribution rate to increase to at least 12%.

Though Lai Ching-te had previously pledged to increase the contribution rate as a campaign pledge, there has not yet been action on the issue.

The demonstration was followed up by another demonstration on October 19th. Labor groups, including the Taoyuan Confederation of Trade Unions, Chunghwa Telecom Union, and other organizations, pledged to strike if their demands were not met, calling for higher wages and an increase in employer contributions to worker pensions.

It is to be if labor becomes a campaign issue ahead of elections next month, then. This does not look likely at present, unless candidates are seeking new issues to brand themselves with, but it can be expected that labor groups will seek to pressure the government on the matter.

author: Chloe Beaton
title: Accessible tram stop campaigners try to board Sydney Road tram
content:
After being ignored by the Victorian government for three-and-a-half years, the Sydney Road Accessible Tram Stops (SATS) campaign held an action on October 23.

A group of about 30 people, with and without mobility aids, attempted to board a tram on Sydney Road to highlight the inaccessibility.

While Sydney Road has many different classes of trams that run along it, campaigners waited for a low floor tram because it is those that would be accessible if tram stops were upgraded.

These could be used by people with mobility aids such as wheelchairs, walkers and crutches, but also by people with prams and shopping trolleys.

The rally waited for more than 20 minutes for a low floor tram to approach. Once it arrived, campaigners tried to board.

Protesters sang and chanted as they unsuccessfully attempted to board the tram.

One person had come with a ramp, and pointed out that the only way someone with a mobility issue could use a tram is to carry around a heavy ramp with them.

To highlight how long the campaign has been going — as well as previous public transport and disability rights campaigns — a model skeleton, named Briony, sat in a wheelchair, was the mascot for the day.

Organisers said “Briony” had been waiting so long for accessible tram stops to be built on Sydney Road that she died in her wheelchair.

While it sounds dramatic, there have been several SATS campaigners who have died before one accessible tram stop has been built on Sydney Road, including Tim Reid and Frank Hall-Bentick.

Campaigners expressed frustration that they have not been acknowledged or heard despite years of campaigning, and federal government legislation stating that all public transport will be accessible in 2022.

They said everyone should be able to access the tram, particularly when the Upfield train line is temporarily closed for level crossing removal, leaving no accessible public transport in the area.

SATS is calling on the Victorian government to guarantee the construction of accessible tram stops on Sydney Road before the Upfield line level crossing removals continue.

[Chloe Beaton is an activist with Sydney Accessible Tram Stops and a Socialist Alliance candidate for Northern Metropolitan in the Victorian elections.]

Sydney Road Accessible Tram Stops Campaign

author: Robert Narai
title: Days of hope and rage in France
content:
At the centre of Paris, the Monument à la République looms over a square that has hosted every great mobilisation of the French left in modern history. The bronze statue of Marianne, symbol of the Republic, holds an olive branch above the words: 

Liberté. Égalité. Fraternité.

 During mass demonstrations on 17 October, dozens of young people scaled the monument while tens of thousands looked on. Some flew Palestinian and red flags. On the statue of 

Egalité

, someone had scrawled “jeunesse dorée” (“gilded youth”, an old term for the idle rich). Marianne herself was draped in a giant yellow vest bearing the words: “The police mutilate high school students”.

For almost a month now, a mass student revolt has been rocking France, in one of the deepest political crises seen in the country in decades. The state that claims to embody liberty, equality and fraternity has answered 

lycéens

 (high schoolers aged 15 to 18) demanding better conditions in schools with tear gas, rubber bullets and mass arrests. That the Republic’s police are maiming young people in the streets is an indictment of the capitalist system the Republic protects.

Days of rage

In response to a national day of action on 17 October, in which an estimated 800,000 people protested across France, the government of Emmanuel Macron unleashed a flurry of violence.

Police fired tear gas into the crowd gathering at Place de la République before the march had formed. Riot police armed with batons, shields and armoured vehicles charged into crowds in Paris, Lyons, Bordeaux and a string of provincial cities, attacking protesters and bystanders alike. According to the Interior Ministry, almost 1,800 people were arrested and more than 500 police were injured, with 855 arrests in Paris alone. A teenager lost a hand in Saint-Étienne and another lost an eye in Mulhouse. Street medics were dragged along the ground by police.

The new element on 17 October was the return of the Yellow Vests, the leaderless movement of rural and provincial workers against fuel taxes and the high cost of living that erupted in 2018, until it was crushed with brute force by the state. After weeks of watching 

lycéens

 face down riot police, the Yellow Vests called their own day of action protesting the cost of living. The Yellow Vests blocked roundabouts and fuel depots from the morning and declared their support for the student revolt. Among them was Pierre, a retiree from Bandol: “I’ve been gassed five times since this morning”, he told 

La Provence

. “[Macron’s government] is declaring war on the people.” The return of the Yellow Vests raises the possibility of the student revolt becoming a rallying point for broader working-class grievances.

Nurses, teachers and firefighters joined the Yellow Vests demonstration. In Lille, 20 rail workers marched together in their SNCF vests. Most of the working class support the movement (55 percent of the French population support the student-led protest movement, according to an Elabe poll) but are not yet part of it.

Whose Republic?

The Macron government’s strategy has been to paint the victims of violence as its perpetrators. Prime Minister Lecornu blamed “far-left groups”, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez targeted “ultra-left individuals”, while Macron declared that “nothing can explain, nothing can excuse” the violence. They pointed to a handful of burnt buildings, such as the town hall in Limoges, to paint a movement of hundreds of thousands as a mindless mob. “The perpetrators directly targeted the institutions of the Republic and the authority of the State”, wrote Bordeaux mayor Thomas Cazenave.

It is worth asking what sort of Republic the mayor of Bordeaux is defending: one in which a burnt town hall causes enormous outrage, but a sixteen-year-old losing an eye to a police grenade prompts hysteria about the need for more law and order.

The ruling class never calls the conditions that produced this revolt violence. Students in France’s poorest schools sit in classrooms infested with cockroaches and rats, in classes of up to 35. Outside school, the police stop, search and arrest young Black and Arab men from the 

banlieues

 (working-class suburbs) for the colour of their skin and the estate they live on, and their operations now cause more than one death per week. Fuel and food prices keep rising, while, according to Oxfam, 53 billionaires own as much as the poorest 48 percent of the population. This is the systematic violence …

author: Alfons Bech, Dick Nichols
title: International convoy seeks to boost solidarity with Ukraine from the bottom up
content:
Alfons Bech is the International Network for Solidarity with Ukraine (INSU) trade union coordinator and a member of the Coordination Group of the International Solidarity Convoy to Ukraine, organising its southern route from Barcelona to Kyiv.

Green Left’s Dick Nichols spoke to Bech about the convoy’s goals and organisation.

Where did the idea of the convoy come from?

It emerged on the second anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion [February 22, 2024], when the European Network for Solidarity with Ukraine (ENSU, now INSU) proposed organising a large international delegation of trade unionists to an event in Kyiv that the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine (FPU) and the Confederation of Free Trade Unions of Ukraine prepared with the support of the European Trade Union Confederation.

Trade unions participated in very large numbers, but online. Only one delegation went to Kyiv, representing the Catalan affiliate of the all-Spanish General Union of Workers (UGT).

The UGT delegation was very shocked by what they saw, but very pleased to have been there in person. They saw the devastation Russia had caused in Bucha and in the neighbourhoods of Kyiv, took part in the distribution of some material aid and got to know a little about Ukrainian culture.

From this, a sort of twinning has developed between the UGT and Ukrainian trade unions, which has been key to our understanding of this war and to the aid effort for Ukraine in Catalonia.

Many aid convoys have already gone to Ukraine. What makes this one different?

This convoy is building on what has already been done at the grassroots level in terms of aid to Ukraine. Nonetheless, this convoy takes place at a crucial moment for Ukraine and Europe.

We are entering the fifth year of a brutal war, and it is not clear how much further attacks the country’s already heavily damaged infrastructure can withstand.

The experience of the past four years shows Ukrainian workers will continue to suffer greatly from always having to repair infrastructure under enemy fire. Russia, conscious of this situation, is preparing to attack even more forcefully what is essential to the survival of the population: energy, cities, hospitals, schools, the bridges of Kyiv, the water supply and the sewerage system

It is a genocidal plan. But it is not being implemented because Russia is doing well in the war or economically. [Vladimir] Putin’s regime faces many difficulties, and these are translating into savage attacks on Ukraine’s civilian population and more repression within Russia.

In this situation of extreme need, we know that any help the convoy can provide, while useful, will be a drop in the ocean.

That is one potent reason why the convoy must have an extra, political, dimension, as a public and visible show of support from the working people of the rest of Europe to their sisters and brothers in Ukraine.

It repeats the cry of the Spanish Civil War, ¡No Pasaran! (They shall not pass) against today’s enemies of human and democratic rights and their chief guarantor, the majority of working people.

We, in Catalonia, cannot bear to see in Ukraine a repeat of the Spanish Republic’s fate, which was abandoned in the face of international fascism. That treachery by great “civilised” powers intent on appeasing [Adolf] Hitler and [Benito] Mussolini cost the peoples of the Spanish state forty years of fascism.

So, the stakes could not be higher…

It is why we in INSU see the need for the sort of sharp expansion of solidarity action that the convoy represents — it is not enough for us to just carry on doing what we have been doing up to now.

What the convoy offers is not only humanitarian or material aid. It is also an instrument for showing that boosted solidarity with Ukraine starts from the bottom up.

This is not just a message about getting more and bigger donations, but of raising awareness about what the overall effort of solidarity with Ukraine must involve.

One critically important example: it is urgent Ukraine receive the €210 billion in frozen Russian assets held by Western financial institutions, such as Euroclear, to fund its defence effort.

While most European governments are looking for ways to cut social spending and increase military spending, these same governments are reluctant to declare the kind of financial war on the Kremlin that would be involved in releasing these assets to Ukraine.

The convoy will be a platform for this and other important messages.
